label: tool:boundary
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{tool:boundary}
Let \(\Omega\) be a smooth bounded planar domain. For \(q\in\partial\Omega\), let \(n(q)\) be the outward unit normal and define the boundary normal coordinates
\[
 \Psi(q,t)=q-tn(q),\qquad q\in\partial\Omega,\quad 0\le t\le\delta_0.
\]
Here \(t\) is the inward normal distance from \(q\). There exists a sufficiently small \(\delta_0>0\), depending only on \(\Omega\), such that every point in the strip \(\{x\in\overline\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\le\delta_0\}\) has a unique representation \(x=\Psi(q,t)\), where \(q\) is the nearest boundary point and
\(\operatorname{dist}(\Psi(q,t),\partial\Omega)=t\). Let \(f\in C^1([0,\infty))\) be nonnegative and nondecreasing. Every positive solution of \(-\Delta v=f(v)\) with zero Dirichlet boundary data has the following property: for each fixed \(q\in\partial\Omega\), the function
\[
 t\longmapsto v(\Psi(q,t))=v(q-tn(q))
\]
is strictly increasing on \([0,\delta_0]\). Moreover, there is a compact set \(K_{\mathrm{peak}}\Subset\Omega\), depending only on \(\Omega\), that contains every critical point, namely every point where \(\nabla v=0\), of every such solution.

label: tool:DTlocal
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{tool:DTlocal}
Let \(v_j>0\) solve \(-\Delta v_j=\theta_jv_je^{v_j^2}\) on \(B_{d_j}(0)\). Assume that \(\theta_j,d_j\) are bounded, \(\beta_j=v_j(0)\to\infty\), and \(\nabla v_j(0)=0\). Set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Uz-mu_j}
    	U(z)=-\log(1+\lvert z\rvert^2/4),\quad\mu_j=(\theta_j\beta_j^2e^{\beta_j^2})^{-1/2}.
    \end{equation}
Assume that
\[
 \mu_j\to0,\qquad d_j/\mu_j\to\infty,
 \qquad \beta_j(v_j(\mu_j z)-\beta_j)\to U(z)
 \quad\hbox{in } C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2),
\]
and that

\begin{equation}\label{eq:DTconditions}
 |x|^2\theta_jv_j^2e^{v_j^2}\le C,
 \qquad |x||\nabla v_j|\le C/\beta_j\quad\hbox{in } B_{d_j}.
\end{equation}
Let \(B_j=B_j(r)\) be the radial solution of the same equation, that is,
\[
 -B_j''(r)-\frac1rB_j'(r)=\theta_jB_j(r)e^{B_j(r)^2}
 \quad(0<r<d_j),\qquad B_j(0)=\beta_j,\quad B_j'(0)=0.
\]
In comparisons on balls, \(B_j(x)\) means \(B_j(|x|)\). Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:DTcomparison}
 \sup_{0\le r\le d_j}|\overline v_j(r)-B_j(r)|=o(\beta_j^{-1}),
 \quad |v_j-B_j|\le C\beta_j^{-1},
 \quad |\nabla(v_j-B_j)|\le\frac{C}{\beta_jd_j},
\end{equation}
where
\[
 \overline v_j(r)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}v_j(re^{i\alpha})\,\mathrm d\alpha
 =\frac1{2\pi r}\int_{\partial B_r}v_j\,\mathrm d\sigma\quad(r>0),
 \qquad \overline v_j(0)=v_j(0).
\]
Set \(t_j(r)=\log(1+r^2/(4\mu_j^2))\). The radial solution has the expansion
\begin{equation}\label{eq:radialexpansion}
 B_j(r)=\beta_j-\frac{t_j(r)}{\beta_j}-\frac{t_j(r)}{\beta_j^3}
 +O(\beta_j^{-2})\qquad(0\le t_j(r)\le\beta_j^2).
\end{equation}

label: tool:chenli
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{tool:chenli}
If \(V\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)\), \(-\Delta V=e^{2V}\), and \(\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2V}<\infty\), then
\[
 V(z)=\log\frac{2\lambda}{1+\lambda^2|z-z_0|^2}
 \quad(\lambda>0, z_0\in\mathbb R^2),
 \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2V}=4\pi.
\]

label: lem:moment
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \cite[Theorem~2.2]{Battaglia2019} with \(G(z,s)=\frac{\theta}{2}a(z)(e^{s^2}-1)\). Then \(\partial_sG(z,v)=\rho_\mathbb D\), and \(G(z,v)=0\) on \(\partial\mathbb D\) because \(v=0\) there. Together with \(a+\frac12z\cdot\nabla a=ag\), this gives \eqref{eq:weighted-pohozaev}.

We next evaluate the boundary integral by Fourier expansion. Write \(b(t)=-\partial_n v(e^{it})\), where \(n\) is the outward unit normal to \(\partial\mathbb D\), and set \(c_n=\int_\mathbb D z^n\rho_\mathbb D(z)\,\mathrm d z\).
The Green representation formula on the disk gives
\[
 b(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\mathbb D K(z,t)\rho_\mathbb D(z)\,\mathrm d z,
 \qquad K(z,t)=\frac{1-|z|^2}{|e^{it}-z|^2}.
\]
The Poisson kernel has the expansion
\[
 K(z,t)=1+\sum_{n\ge1}(z^ne^{-int}+\overline z^{\,n}e^{int}).
\]
Since \(K\ge0\) and \(\int_0^{2\pi}K(z,t)\,\mathrm d t=2\pi\), we have
\(\int_\mathbb D\int_0^{2\pi}K\rho_\mathbb D\,\mathrm d t\,\mathrm d z=2\pi M<\infty\). Fubini's theorem and orthogonality yield
\[
 \int_0^{2\pi}b(t)\,\mathrm d t=M,
 \qquad \int_0^{2\pi}b(t)e^{int}\,\mathrm d t=c_n\quad(n\ge1).
\]
The function \(b\) is smooth and real-valued, so its positive and negative frequency coefficients are complex conjugates. Parseval's identity therefore gives
\[
 \int_0^{2\pi}b(t)^2\,\mathrm d t
 =2\pi\left[\left|\frac M{2\pi}\right|^2
       +2\sum_{n\ge1}\left|\frac{c_n}{2\pi}\right|^2\right]
 =\frac1{2\pi}\left(M^2+2\sum_{n\ge1}|c_n|^2\right).
\]

Substituting Parseval's identity into \eqref{eq:weighted-pohozaev}, we obtain
\[
 \int_\mathbb D gP_\mathbb D\,\mathrm d z
 =\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}b(t)^2\,\mathrm d t
 =\frac1{4\pi}\left(M^2+2\sum_{n\ge1}|c_n|^2\right),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:moment}.

label: lem:mass
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:int_Omega-P-dx
title: Proof
body_md:
Testing the equation {with} a positive first Dirichlet eigenfunction \(\varphi_1\), we obtain
\[
 \theta\int_\Omega ue^{u^2}\varphi_1
 =\lambda_1(\Omega)\int_\Omega u\varphi_1
 >\theta\int_\Omega u\varphi_1,
\]
Thus \(\theta<\lambda_1(\Omega)\). By \eqref{eq:pressure-comparison},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:int_Omega-P-dx}
 \int_\Omega P\,\mathrm d x\le\int_\Omega\rho\,\mathrm d x=M.
\end{equation}
Set \(C_0=4\pi G_*\). The integral identity \eqref{eq:moment} gives
\[
 M^2\le4\pi\int_\mathbb D gP_\mathbb D
 \le C_0\int_\Omega P\le C_0M,
\]
and therefore \(M\le C_0\).

For any \(T>1\), use \(P\le\theta e^{T^2}\) on \(\{u\le T\}\) and \eqref{eq:pressure-comparison} on \(\{u>T\}\) to obtain
\[
 M^2\le C_0\left(|\Omega|\theta e^{T^2}+\frac MT\right)
 \le C_0|\Omega|\theta e^{T^2}+\frac12M^2+\frac{C_0^2}{2T^2}.
\]
For \(0<\theta<e^{-2}\), choose \(T=\sqrt{\log(1/\theta)/2}\). Then
\[
 M^2\le\frac{2C_0^2}{\log(1/\theta)}+2C_0|\Omega|\sqrt\theta
 \le\frac{C_\Omega}{\log(1/\theta)}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:massbounds}. If \(\theta_j\to0\), then \(M_j\to0\). For every finite \(q\), Minkowski's inequality and \eqref{eq:greenbounds} give
\[
 \|u_j\|_{L^q(\Omega)}
 \le\int_\Omega\|G(\cdot,y)\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y
 \le C_{q,\Omega}M_j\to0.
\]
This completes the proof.

label: lem:strip
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the normal coordinates of Theorem~\ref{tool:boundary}, decrease \(\delta_0\) so that the area element satisfies
\[
 \,\mathrm d x=J(q,t)\,\mathrm d\sigma(q)\,\mathrm d t,
 \qquad \tfrac12\le J(q,t)\le\tfrac32\quad(0\le t\le\delta_0).
\]
Let \(F\ge0\) be nondecreasing along inward normals, and set \(S_\varepsilon=\{d<\varepsilon\}\). Then
\[
 \int_0^\varepsilon F(\Psi(q,t))J(q,t)\,\mathrm d t
 \le\tfrac32\varepsilon F(\Psi(q,\varepsilon)),\qquad
 \int_\varepsilon^{\delta_0}F(\Psi(q,t))J(q,t)\,\mathrm d t
 \ge\tfrac12(\delta_0-\varepsilon)F(\Psi(q,\varepsilon)).
\]
Integrating in \(q\) and writing \(I_\varepsilon=\int_{S_\varepsilon}F\), \(T=\int_\Omega F\), we obtain
\[
 (\delta_0-\varepsilon)I_\varepsilon\le3\varepsilon(T-I_\varepsilon),
 \qquad I_\varepsilon\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{\delta_0+2\varepsilon}T\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{\delta_0}T.
\]
Boundary monotonicity shows that \(\rho_j\) and \(P_j\), defined in \eqref{eq:notation}, satisfy these conditions. Applying the estimate to each and dividing by \(M_j\) and \(M_j^2\), respectively, proves \eqref{eq:strip}.

label: lem:jensen
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(w_j=G\nu_j\) and \(\nu_j(\Omega)=1\), Jensen's inequality and \eqref{eq:greenbounds} give
\[
 e^{\alpha w_j(x)}
 \le\int_\Omega e^{\alpha G(x,y)}\,\mathrm d\nu_j(y)
 \le\int_\Omega\left(\frac{L_0}{|x-y|}\right)^{\alpha/(2\pi)}\,\mathrm d\nu_j(y).
\]
The singularity can be handled by first truncating \(G\) and then applying monotone convergence. Since \(\alpha/(2\pi)<2\), integration in polar coordinates gives
\[
 K_{\alpha,\Omega}:=\sup_{y\in\Omega}
 \int_\Omega\left(\frac{L_0}{|x-y|}\right)^{\alpha/(2\pi)}\,\mathrm d x<\infty.
\]
Integrating in \(x\) and applying Tonelli's theorem proves \eqref{eq:globaljensen}.

For the local estimate, abbreviate \(B_r=B_r(x_0)\) and set \(m_j=\nu_j(B_{2r})\). The weak convergence inequality for closed sets gives
\[
 \limsup_jm_j\le\nu(\overline B_{2r})<\bar p.
\]
Split the integral defining \(w_j=G\nu_j\) as \(w_j=a_j+b_j\), where
\[
 a_j(x)=\int_{B_{2r}}G(x,y)\,\mathrm d\nu_j(y),\qquad
 b_j(x)=\int_{\Omega\setminus B_{2r}}G(x,y)\,\mathrm d\nu_j(y).
\]
For \(x\in B_r\), the second term satisfies
\(0\le b_j(x)\le(2\pi)^{-1}\log(L_0/r)\). For all sufficiently large \(j\), the measure
\(\nu_j|_{B_{2r}}/\bar p\) has mass less than one. {Add a point to the domain of integration}, assign it mass \(1-m_j/\bar p\), and define the kernel to be zero there. Jensen's inequality for the resulting probability measure yields
\[
 e^{(\alpha/\bar p)a_j(x)}
 \le1-\frac{m_j}{\bar p}
 +\frac1{\bar p}\int_{B_{2r}}e^{\alpha G(x,y)}\,\mathrm d\nu_j(y).
\]
The integral of the right-hand side over \(B_r\) is at most \(|B_r|+K_{\alpha,\Omega}\). Together with the bound for \(b_j\), this proves \eqref{eq:localjensen}.

We now estimate the densities on \(\{s_j\le L\}\). Suppose that a measurable set \(D\subset\Omega\) satisfies
\(\int_D e^{\Lambda w_j}\le C\) for a fixed \(\Lambda>0\). On \(\{s_j\le L\}\), the identities \(u_j^2=s_jw_j\) and \(e^t-1\le te^t\) give
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d\nu_j}{\,\mathrm d x}=\theta_jw_je^{u_j^2}\le\theta_jw_je^{Lw_j},
 \qquad
 \frac{\,\mathrm d\Pi_j}{\,\mathrm d x}\le\theta_jw_j^2e^{u_j^2}\le\theta_jw_j^2e^{Lw_j}.
\]
If \(q\ge1\) and \(qL<\Lambda\), then
\((t^q+t^{2q})e^{qLt}\le C_{q,L,\Lambda}e^{\Lambda t}\), hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lowheight-Lq}
 \left\|\mathbf 1_{\{s_j\le L\}}\frac{\,\mathrm d\nu_j}{\,\mathrm d x}\right\|_{L^q(D)}
 +\left\|\mathbf 1_{\{s_j\le L\}}\frac{\,\mathrm d\Pi_j}{\,\mathrm d x}\right\|_{L^q(D)}
 \le C_{D,q,L,\Lambda}\theta_j.
\end{equation}
Taking \(D=B_r(x_0)\), \(\Lambda=\alpha/\bar p\), and \(q=1\) proves \eqref{eq:lowheight}.
head: environment

label: rem:global-lowheight
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:global-lowheight}
For \(D=\Omega\), \eqref{eq:globaljensen} shows that \eqref{eq:lowheight-Lq} holds whenever \(qL<4\pi\). In particular, for \(0<L<4\pi\),
\[
 \nu_j(\{s_j\le L\})+\Pi_j(\{s_j\le L\})\le C_{L,\Omega}\theta_j.
\]
In either the global or local setting above, combining \eqref{eq:lowheight-Lq} with \(q=1\) and \eqref{eq:pressure-comparison} gives, for every bounded nonnegative function \(\psi\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pressure-split}
 \int_D\psi\,\mathrm d\Pi_j
 \le C_{D,L}\|\psi\|_\infty\theta_j
   +\frac1L\int_D\psi\,\mathrm d\nu_j.
\end{equation}
The global estimate requires \(L<4\pi\), and the local estimate requires \(L<4\pi/\bar p\). The constants also depend on the gap between the chosen exponent and its critical value.

label: lem:budget
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The relation \(\log\theta_j=o(\beta_j^2)\) and the definition of \(\mu_j\) give
\(\log(1/\mu_j)=\beta_j^2/2+o(\beta_j^2)\). Hence \(\mu_j/d_j\to0\) and \(d_j/L_j\to0\). It remains to prove the two bounds in \eqref{eq:DTconditions}.

Fix \(T>0\), and set \(m_T=\int_{B_T}e^{2U}>0\). Changing variables by \(x=x_j+\mu_jz\) and using the assumed \(C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}\) convergence, we obtain
\(\beta_j\int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}\rho_j\to m_T\).
If \(z\in B_{L_j}(x_j)\) and \(y\in B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)\), then \(|z-y|\le2L_j\) for all sufficiently large \(j\). By \eqref{eq:green},
\[
 G(z,y)\ge\frac1{2\pi}\log\frac1{2L_j}-C_K
 =\frac{\beta_j^2}{64\pi}-O_K(1).
\]
Since \(G\ge0\) and \(\rho_j\ge0\), retaining only the integral over \(B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)\) in the Green representation formula gives
\[
 u_j(z)\ge\left(\frac{\beta_j^2}{64\pi}-C\right)
 \frac{m_T+o(1)}{\beta_j}\ge c\beta_j.
\]
Using \eqref{eq:budget}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:budgetlower}
 u_j\ge c\beta_j\quad\hbox{in }B_{L_j}(x_j),\qquad
 \int_{B_{L_j}(x_j)}\rho_j\,\mathrm d x
 \le\frac1{c\beta_j}\int_{B_{L_j}(x_j)}u_j\rho_j\,\mathrm d x
 \le\frac C{\beta_j}.
\end{equation}

Set \(V_j=\theta_ju_j^2e^{u_j^2}=u_j\rho_j\), and define on \(\overline B_{L_j}(x_j)\)
\(D_j(z)=\min\{|z-x_j|,L_j-|z-x_j|\}\).
We first prove that \(\sup_{\overline B_{L_j}(x_j)}D_j^2V_j\le C\). Otherwise, pass to a subsequence and choose \(y_j\) where the continuous function \(D_j^2V_j\) attains its maximum on the closed ball, with
\[
 D_j(y_j)^2V_j(y_j)
 =\max_{y\in\overline B_{L_j}(x_j)}D_j(y)^2V_j(y)\to\infty.
\]
Set \(b_j=u_j(y_j)\) and \(\widehat\mu_j=V_j(y_j)^{-1/2}\). Since \(D_j(y_j)\le L_j\to0\), we have \(V_j(y_j)\to\infty\). Boundedness of \(\theta_j\) and the identity \(V_j(y_j)=\theta_jb_j^2e^{b_j^2}\) then give \(b_j\to\infty\). Also,
\[
 \frac{\widehat\mu_j}{D_j(y_j)}
 =\frac1{\sqrt{D_j(y_j)^2V_j(y_j)}}\to0.
\]
Fix \(T>0\). For all sufficiently large \(j\), \(T\widehat\mu_j<D_j(y_j)\le L_j-|y_j-x_j|\), so \(y_j+\widehat\mu_jz\in B_{L_j}(x_j)\) whenever \(|z|\le T\). The definition of \(D_j\) gives \(|D_j(y)-D_j(y')|\le|y-y'|\); hence
\[
 D_j(y_j+\widehat\mu_jz)\ge D_j(y_j)-T\widehat\mu_j>0.
\]
Substituting \(y_j+\widehat\mu_jz\) into \(D_j(y)^2V_j(y)\le D_j(y_j)^2V_j(y_j)\), we obtain
\[
 \frac{V_j(y_j+\widehat\mu_j z)}{V_j(y_j)}
 \le\left(\frac{D_j(y_j)}{D_j(y_j+\widehat\mu_jz)}\right)^2
 \le\left(1-\frac{T\widehat\mu_j}{D_j(y_j)}\right)^{-2}
 =1+o(1).
\]
The final error is independent of \(z\), so the estimate is uniform on each fixed ball. If \(u_j(y_j+\widehat\mu_j z)>b_j\), taking logarithms gives \(u_j^2-b_j^2\le o(1)\). If \(u_j(y_j+\widehat\mu_j z)\le b_j\), then \(u_j^2-b_j^2\le0\). Therefore
\[
 \zeta_j(z):=b_j(u_j(y_j+\widehat\mu_j z)-b_j)\le o(1),\qquad
 \zeta_j(0)=0,\qquad
 0\le-\Delta\zeta_j=\frac{u_j}{b_j}e^{u_j^2-b_j^2}\le1+o(1).
\]
Here \(\Delta\) acts on \(z\), and every occurrence of \(u_j\) on the right is evaluated at \(y_j+\widehat\mu_jz\). The local \(W^{2,q}\) and Schauder estimates at the beginning of this subsection give a subsequential limit \(\zeta\) satisfying \(-\Delta\zeta=e^{2\zeta}\) and \(\zeta\le0=\zeta(0)\). For fixed \(T>0\), make the change of variables \(x=y_j+\widehat\mu_jz\) on \(B_{T\widehat\mu_j}(y_j)\). Since \(\widehat\mu_j^2V_j(y_j+\widehat\mu_jz)\to e^{2\zeta(z)}\), this ball lies in \(B_{L_j}(x_j)\), and \eqref{eq:budget} holds, Fatou's lemma gives \(\int_{B_T}e^{2\zeta}\le4\pi\). Letting \(T\to\infty\) and applying monotone convergence yields \(\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\zeta}\le4\pi\). Theorem~\ref{tool:chenli} therefore implies \(\zeta=U\) and \(\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2U}=4\pi\).
The distance between the two centers tends to infinity relative to either rescaling parameter. First, \(D_j(y_j)\le|y_j-x_j|\) gives \(|y_j-x_j|/\widehat\mu_j\to\infty\). If \(|y_j-x_j|/\mu_j\) were bounded along a subsequence, \eqref{eq:localassumptions} and \eqref{eq:Uz-mu_j} would give \(\mu_j^2V_j(y_j)=O(1)\). Together with \(D_j(y_j)\le|y_j-x_j|\le C\mu_j\), this would imply \(D_j(y_j)^2V_j(y_j)=O(1)\), contrary to the choice of \(y_j\).
Thus, for fixed \(T\), the balls \(B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)\) and \(B_{T\widehat\mu_j}(y_j)\) are eventually disjoint.
Since \(\mu_j/L_j\to0\) and \(T\widehat\mu_j<D_j(y_j)\le L_j-|y_j-x_j|\), both balls lie in \(B_{L_j}(x_j)\). The changes of variables \(x=x_j+\mu_jz\) and \(x=y_j+\widehat\mu_jz\), together with local convergence of the two rescaled functions, show that the integral of \(u_j\rho_j\) over each ball tends to \(m_T\). Disjointness and \(u_j\rho_j\ge0\) give
\[
 \liminf_j\int_{B_{L_j}(x_j)}u_j\rho_j\ge2m_T.
\]

Taking \(T\) large enough that \(2m_T>4\pi\) contradicts \eqref{eq:budget}. Hence \(\sup D_j^2V_j\le C\). Since \(D_j(z)=|z-x_j|\) on \(B_{L_j/2}(x_j)\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointbudget}
 |z-x_j|^2\theta_ju_j(z)^2e^{u_j(z)^2}\le C.
\end{equation}

Because \(d_j/L_j\to0\), we have \(3d_j<L_j\) for all sufficiently large \(j\), and \eqref{eq:pointbudget} holds on \(B_{d_j}(x_j)\). To prove the gradient estimate, fix \(z\) with \(r=|z-x_j|\in(0,d_j]\). If \(y\in B_{r/2}(z)\), then \(r/2\le|y-x_j|\le3r/2\), and \(B_{r/2}(z)\subset B_{L_j/2}(x_j)\). Thus \eqref{eq:budgetlower} and \eqref{eq:pointbudget} imply \(\rho_j\le C/(\beta_jr^2)\) on this ball. {In the Green representation formula for the gradient, split the domain of integration into} \(B_{r/2}(z)\), \(B_{L_j}(x_j)\setminus B_{r/2}(z)\), and \(\Omega\setminus B_{L_j}(x_j)\). By \eqref{eq:greenbounds}, the absolute values of these three contributions satisfy, respectively,
\[
 \frac{C}{\beta_jr^2}\int_{B_{r/2}(z)}\frac{\,\mathrm d y}{|z-y|}
 \le\frac{C}{\beta_jr},\qquad
 \frac Cr\int_{B_{L_j}(x_j)}\rho_j\le\frac{C}{\beta_jr},\qquad
 \frac{CM_j}{L_j}.
\]
Since \(\sup_jM_j<\infty\),
\[
 \beta_jM_j\frac{d_j}{L_j}\le C\beta_je^{-\beta_j^2/32}\to0,
\]
the outer integral is also at most \(C/(\beta_jr)\). Together with \eqref{eq:pointbudget}, this proves \eqref{eq:DTconditions}. All remaining hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{tool:DTlocal} follow from the assumptions of the lemma.

title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:tlog
title: Proof
body_md:
Set \(\ell_j=\log(\theta_j\beta_j^2/4)=o(\beta_j^2)\). At the comparison radius, the logarithmic variable in the radial expansion satisfies
\(t_j(d_j)=\tfrac78\beta_j^2+\ell_j+o(1)<\beta_j^2\) for all sufficiently large \(j\). On any fixed closed subinterval of \((1/16,1/2)\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tlog}
 t_j(r_j(\tau))=(1-2\tau)\beta_j^2+\ell_j+O(e^{-c\beta_j^2})
\end{equation}
uniformly, for some \(c>0\). Thus \eqref{eq:radialexpansion} applies at these radii.
Let \(m_j(r)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}u_j(x_j+re^{i\alpha})\,\mathrm d\alpha\) be the circular mean about \(x_j\). Integrating the equation over a ball gives
\(-2\pi r m_j'(r)=Q_j(r)\). Since \(\rho_j>0\), the function \(Q_j(r)=\int_{B_r(x_j)}\rho_j\) is nondecreasing. Choose fixed numbers \(1/16<\tau_-<\tau<\tau_+<1/2\), and set \(r_-=r_j(\tau_+)\), \(r=r_j(\tau)\), and \(r_+=r_j(\tau_-)\). Integrating \(-2\pi m_j'(t)=Q_j(t)/t\) over \([r_-,r]\) and \([r,r_+]\), and using monotonicity of \(Q_j\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:secants}
 \frac{2\pi[m_j(r_-)-m_j(r)]}{\log(r/r_-)}
 \le Q_j(r)\le
 \frac{2\pi[m_j(r)-m_j(r_+)]}{\log(r_+/r)}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:DTcomparison}, \eqref{eq:radialexpansion}, and \eqref{eq:tlog}, at each of the three radii,
\[
 m_j(r)=\beta_j-
 \left(\frac1{\beta_j}+\frac1{\beta_j^3}\right)
 (\beta_j^2+\ell_j+2\log r)+o(\beta_j^{-1}).
\]
Upon subtraction, the constant terms arising from \(\beta_j^2+\ell_j\) cancel. For example,
\[
 m_j(r_-)-m_j(r)
 =\left(\frac2{\beta_j}+\frac2{\beta_j^3}\right)\log(r/r_-)
   +o(\beta_j^{-1}).
\]
Dividing by \(\log(r/r_-)=(\tau_+-\tau)\beta_j^2\) gives an error of precisely \(o(\beta_j^{-3})\).
The quotient on the right of \eqref{eq:secants} has the same expansion. Since \(Q_j(r)\) lies between the two quotients, it satisfies \eqref{eq:flux}.

The same expansion of the function gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:meanexpansion}
 m_j(r_j(\tau))=2\tau\beta_j-
 \frac{\ell_j+1-2\tau}{\beta_j}+o(\beta_j^{-1});
\end{equation}
where \(\ell_j/\beta_j^3=o(\beta_j^{-1})\).
For each fixed \(y\), the circular mean of \(\log|x_j+re^{it}-y|\) is \(\log\max\{r,|x_j-y|\}\), while that of \(H(\cdot,y)\) is \(H(x_j,y)\). Substituting these two mean-value identities into the Green representation formula for \(u_j\) and interchanging the order of integration gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:circleexact}
 m_j(r)=\frac{Q_j(r)}{2\pi}\log\frac1r
 -\int_{B_r(x_j)}H(x_j,y)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y
 +I_{\mathrm{out},j}(r).
\end{equation}
The integral involving the regular part equals \(R(x_j)Q_j(r)+O(rQ_j(r))=4\pi R(x_j)/\beta_j+o(\beta_j^{-1})\). By \eqref{eq:flux}, the first term is \(2\tau\beta_j+2\tau/\beta_j+o(\beta_j^{-1})\). Substituting into \eqref{eq:circleexact} and comparing with \eqref{eq:meanexpansion}, we obtain
\[
 2\tau\beta_j-\frac{\ell_j+1-2\tau}{\beta_j}
 =2\tau\beta_j+\frac{2\tau-4\pi R(x_j)}{\beta_j}
   +I_{\mathrm{out},j}(r_j(\tau))+o(\beta_j^{-1}).
\]
Cancelling \(2\tau\beta_j\), multiplying by \(\beta_j\), and rearranging proves \eqref{eq:matching}.

label: lem:maxbubble
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{tool:boundary}, the points \(x_j\) lie in a fixed compact subset of \(\Omega\). Lemma~\ref{lem:logtheta} gives \(\log(1/\mu_j)/\gamma_j^2\to1/2\), so the rescaled domains exhaust \(\mathbb R^2\).
The functions \(\eta_j=\gamma_j(u_j(x_j+\mu_jz)-\gamma_j)\) satisfy
\[
 \eta_j\le0=\eta_j(0),\qquad
 0\le-\Delta\eta_j=
 \left(1+\frac{\eta_j}{\gamma_j^2}\right)
 e^{2\eta_j+\eta_j^2/\gamma_j^2}\le1.
\]
The local \(W^{2,q}\) and Schauder estimates at the beginning of the section give a subsequential limit \(\eta\) satisfying \(-\Delta\eta=e^{2\eta}\) and \(\eta\le0=\eta(0)\).
In the Green representation formula at \(x_j\), retain only the integral over a fixed rescaled ball to obtain
\[
 1\ge\int_{B_T}\frac{G(x_j,x_j+\mu_jz)}{\gamma_j^2}
 \frac{u_j(x_j+\mu_jz)}{\gamma_j}
 e^{u_j(x_j+\mu_jz)^2-\gamma_j^2}\,\mathrm d z.
\]
where
\[
 \frac{G(x_j,x_j+\mu_jz)}{\gamma_j^2}
 =\frac{\log(1/\mu_j)}{2\pi\gamma_j^2}
  -\frac{\log|z|}{2\pi\gamma_j^2}
  -\frac{H(x_j,x_j+\mu_jz)}{\gamma_j^2},
\]
The first term tends to \(1/(4\pi)\); the other two tend to zero uniformly on each fixed annulus \(\{\varepsilon\le|z|\le T\}\), \(0<\varepsilon<T\).
First exclude a small ball about the origin, use positivity to take the lower limit, and then shrink the excluded ball. This gives
\(1\ge(4\pi)^{-1}\int_{B_T}e^{2\eta}\). Let \(T\to\infty\). Theorem~\ref{tool:chenli}, together with \(\eta\le0=\eta(0)\), yields \(\eta=U\). Every subsequence has a further convergent subsequence with this limit, so \eqref{eq:maxbubble} holds for the full sequence.

Set \(m_T=\int_{B_T}e^{2U}\uparrow4\pi\) and \(r_j=e^{-\sigma\gamma_j^2}\). Under the change of variables \(y=x_j+\mu_jz\), we have
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \gamma_j\mu_j^2\rho_j(x_j+\mu_jz)
 &=\frac{u_j(x_j+\mu_jz)}{\gamma_j}
   e^{u_j(x_j+\mu_jz)^2-\gamma_j^2}\to e^{2U(z)},\\
 \mu_j^2u_j\rho_j(x_j+\mu_jz)
 &=\left(\frac{u_j(x_j+\mu_jz)}{\gamma_j}\right)^2
   e^{u_j(x_j+\mu_jz)^2-\gamma_j^2}\to e^{2U(z)}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
In the second line, \(u_j\) is also evaluated at \(x_j+\mu_jz\). These densities are uniformly bounded on fixed balls.
Since \(\int_{B_T}|\log|z||\,\mathrm d z<\infty\), we may also pass to the limit in the integral with the Green kernel. Thus
\[
 \gamma_j\int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}\rho_j\to m_T,
 \quad \int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}u_j\rho_j\to m_T,
 \quad \frac1{\gamma_j}\int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}G(x_j,y)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y\to\frac{m_T}{4\pi}.
\]
On \(B_{r_j}(x_j)\setminus B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)\), the Green function is at least \(\sigma\gamma_j^2/(2\pi)-C\). Subtracting the inner contribution from the Green representation formula and discarding the nonnegative outer contribution gives
\[
 \limsup_j\gamma_j\int_{B_{r_j}(x_j)\setminus B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}\rho_j
 \le\frac{2\pi}{\sigma}\left(1-\frac{m_T}{4\pi}\right).
\]
Letting \(T\to\infty\) proves the first assertion of \eqref{eq:maxbudget}. Since \(u_j\le\gamma_j\), the upper limit of the weighted integral is at most \(4\pi\), while convergence of the integral on small balls gives a lower limit of at least \(4\pi\). This proves the second assertion.

label: eq:maxmatching
title: Proof
body_md:
If \(\gamma_j\to\infty\), Lemmas~\ref{lem:logtheta} and \ref{lem:maxbubble} verify all hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:budget}, including \eqref{eq:budget} with \(\sigma=1/32\). Taking \(\tau=1/4\) in Lemma~\ref{lem:matching}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maxmatching}
 \log(\theta_j\gamma_j^2/4)
 =4\pi R(x_j)-1-\gamma_j I_{\mathrm{out},j}(e^{-\gamma_j^2/4})+o(1).
\end{equation}
Since \(G\ge0\) and \(\rho_j\ge0\), we have \(I_{\mathrm{out},j}(e^{-\gamma_j^2/4})\ge0\). The function \(R\) is bounded on the fixed compact set containing all maximum points, so \(\theta_j\gamma_j^2\) is bounded. {If \eqref{eq:maxbound} failed for the full family of solutions, we could choose a sequence with \(\theta_j\gamma_j^2\to\infty\). Since \(\theta_j<\lambda_1(\Omega)\), this would force \(\gamma_j\to\infty\), contradicting the preceding bound.}

By \eqref{eq:strip}, there is a compact set \(K_1\Subset\Omega\), independent of the solution, such that \(\int_{K_1}\rho\,\mathrm d x\ge M/2\). Recall that \(K_{\mathrm{peak}}\Subset\Omega\) is the fixed compact set from Theorem~\ref{tool:boundary}, depending only on \(\Omega\) and containing all critical points of every positive solution, in particular each maximum point \(x_j\). The Green function has a positive lower bound \(g_0\) on \(K_{\mathrm{peak}}\times K_1\): away from the diagonal this follows from compactness and positivity, while near the diagonal \(G\) tends to \(+\infty\). Abbreviate \(Q_j=Q_j(e^{-\gamma_j^2/4})\) and \(I_{\mathrm{out},j}=I_{\mathrm{out},j}(e^{-\gamma_j^2/4})\). Then
\[
 I_{\mathrm{out},j}\ge g_0(M_j/2-Q_j),\qquad
 \gamma_jQ_j=4\pi+o(1).
\]
Substituting this lower bound into \eqref{eq:maxmatching} and rearranging gives, for all sufficiently large \(j\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \frac{g_0}2\gamma_jM_j
 &\le\gamma_j I_{\mathrm{out},j}+g_0\gamma_jQ_j\\
 &=4\pi R(x_j)-1-\log(\theta_j\gamma_j^2/4)
   +g_0\gamma_jQ_j+o(1)\\
 &\le C+\log^+(1/(\theta_j\gamma_j^2)).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus
    \[\gamma_jM_j\le C_\Omega[1+\log^+(1/(\theta_j\gamma_j^2))].\]
{This estimate holds for all solutions with a constant depending only on \(\Omega\). Otherwise, choose solutions for which
\[
 \frac{\gamma_jM_j}{1+\log^+(1/(\theta_j\gamma_j^2))}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Since \(M_j\le C_\Omega\), necessarily \(\gamma_j\to\infty\), contradicting the estimate just proved.}

If \(\gamma\ge1\), then \(\log^+(1/(\theta\gamma^2))\le\log^+(1/\theta)\). If \(0<\gamma<1\), the mass estimate gives \(\gamma M\le M\le C_\Omega\). Together with \(E\le\gamma M\), these bounds yield \eqref{eq:logenergy}.

 Finally, \(E_j\to\infty\) implies \(\gamma_j\to\infty\), and \eqref{eq:maxbound} then gives \(\theta_j\to0\).

label: lem:boundary-zero
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:boundary-zero}
Regard \(\nu_j,\Pi_j\) as measures on \(\overline\Omega\), following the extension convention in Section~\ref{sec:notation}. There is a common subsequence such that
\[
 \nu_j\rightharpoonup\nu,\qquad \Pi_j\rightharpoonup\Pi
 \quad\hbox{on }\overline\Omega.
\]
Every such pair of weak limits satisfies
\[
 \nu(\partial\Omega)=\Pi(\partial\Omega)=0,
 \qquad \nu(\Omega)=1.
\]
In particular, \(\nu\) is a probability measure on \(\Omega\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set \(K=\sup_j\Pi_j(\Omega)<\infty\). Since \(\overline\Omega\) is compact and
\(\nu_j(\overline\Omega)=1\), \(\Pi_j(\overline\Omega)\le K\), weak compactness of finite nonnegative measures gives a common subsequence such that
\(\nu_j\rightharpoonup\nu\) and \(\Pi_j\rightharpoonup\Pi\), where \(\nu,\Pi\) are finite nonnegative measures on \(\overline\Omega\).

Let \(d\) be the distance function from Lemma~\ref{lem:strip}. Fix \(0<\varepsilon<\delta_0\), and define
\[
 \chi_\varepsilon(x)=\max\left\{1-\frac{d(x)}{\varepsilon},0\right\},
 \qquad x\in\overline\Omega.
\]
Then \(\chi_\varepsilon\in C(\overline\Omega)\), \(0\le\chi_\varepsilon\le1\), and \(\chi_\varepsilon\) equals \(1\) on \(\partial\Omega\) and \(0\) on
\(\{d\ge\varepsilon\}\). Testing weak convergence with \(\chi_\varepsilon\) and using the boundary strip estimate \eqref{eq:strip}, we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
  \nu(\partial\Omega)
  &\le\int_{\overline\Omega}\chi_\varepsilon\,\mathrm d\nu
  =\lim_{j\to\infty}\int_{\overline\Omega}\chi_\varepsilon\,\mathrm d\nu_j
  \le C_\Omega\varepsilon,\\
  \Pi(\partial\Omega)
  &\le\int_{\overline\Omega}\chi_\varepsilon\,\mathrm d\Pi
  =\lim_{j\to\infty}\int_{\overline\Omega}\chi_\varepsilon\,\mathrm d\Pi_j
  \le C_\Omega K\varepsilon.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before \(j\to\infty\). Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) gives
\(\nu(\partial\Omega)=\Pi(\partial\Omega)=0\). Finally, testing weak convergence with the constant function \(1\) yields
\[
 \nu(\overline\Omega)=\lim_{j\to\infty}\nu_j(\overline\Omega)=1.
\]
Thus \(\nu(\Omega)=\nu(\overline\Omega)-\nu(\partial\Omega)=1\).

label: lem:pressureupper
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:local-pressure-domination
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix \(B_{2r}(x_0)\Subset\Omega\), \(\bar p>\nu(\overline B_{2r}(x_0))\), and
\(0<L<4\pi/\bar p\). For a nonnegative \(\psi\in C_c(B_r(x_0))\), letting \(j\to\infty\) in \eqref{eq:pressure-split} gives
\[
 \int\psi\,\mathrm d\Pi\le L^{-1}\int\psi\,\mathrm d\nu.
\]
Letting first \(L\uparrow4\pi/\bar p\) and then \(\bar p\downarrow\nu(\overline B_{2r}(x_0))\), we obtain the local measure inequality
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-pressure-domination}
 \Pi|_{B_r(x_0)}
 \le\frac{\nu(\overline B_{2r}(x_0))}{4\pi}\,\nu|_{B_r(x_0)}.
\end{equation}
This argument also covers the case in which the coefficient on the right is zero. Similarly, in the global version of \eqref{eq:pressure-split}, letting first \(j\to\infty\) and then \(L\uparrow4\pi\) yields \(\Pi\le\nu/(4\pi)\). Thus \(\Pi\ll\nu\). By the Radon--Nikodym theorem, we may write
\(\Pi=f\nu\), where \(f\) is a nonnegative Borel function and \(0\le f\le1/(4\pi)\) holds \(\nu\)-almost everywhere.

To make all local upper bounds hold outside a single null set, consider the countable family of balls
\[
 \mathcal B=\{B_r(x_0):x_0\in\mathbb Q^2,\ r\in\mathbb Q,
 \ r>0,\ \overline B_{2r}(x_0)\subset\Omega\}.
\]
For each \(B=B_r(x_0)\in\mathcal B\), \eqref{eq:local-pressure-domination} implies
\(f\le c_B:=\nu(\overline B_{2r}(x_0))/(4\pi)\) \(\nu\)-almost everywhere on \(B\).
Indeed, applying the measure inequality to \(F_m=\{x\in B:f(x)>c_B+1/m\}\) gives \(\nu(F_m)=0\).
Taking the union over all \(B\in\mathcal B\) and \(m\ge1\), we obtain a \(\nu\)-null set \(N\) outside which all these bounds hold simultaneously.

Fix \(x\notin N\). Choose rational numbers \(r_n\downarrow0\) and points \(x_n\in\mathbb Q^2\) such that
\(3r_n<\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\) and \(|x_n-x|<r_n/2\). Then
\(x\in B_{r_n}(x_n)\in\mathcal B\), and
\[
 0\le f(x)\le\frac{\nu(\overline B_{2r_n}(x_n))}{4\pi}
 \le\frac{\nu(\overline B_{3r_n}(x))}{4\pi}
 \longrightarrow\frac{\nu(\{x\})}{4\pi}.
\]
The last step uses continuity from above for finite measures. Thus \(f\) vanishes almost everywhere away from the atoms.

The set \(\mathcal A=\{x:\nu(\{x\})>0\}\) is at most countable: for each \(m\ge1\), there are at most \(m\) points with mass at least \(1/m\). Hence
\[
 \Pi(\Omega\setminus\mathcal A)=\int_{\Omega\setminus\mathcal A}f\,\mathrm d\nu=0,
 \qquad \Pi=\sum_i\tau_i\delta_{a_i}.
\]
Every atom lies outside \(N\), so
\(0\le\tau_i=f(a_i)p_i\le p_i^2/(4\pi)\), proving \eqref{eq:pressureupper}.

label: lem:stress
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:intpho_jXcdotnablau_j
title: Proof
body_md:
First suppose that \(X\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)\). The chain rule gives
\(\nabla P_j=2\theta_ju_je^{u_j^2}\nabla u_j=2\rho_j\nabla u_j\). Hence
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:intpho_jXcdotnablau_j}
    	\int_\Omega\rho_jX\cdot\nabla u_j
    	=\frac12\int_\Omega X\cdot\nabla P_j
    	=-\frac12\int_\Omega P_j\operatorname{div} X.
    \end{equation}
Differentiating the Green representation formula and using \eqref{eq:green}, we obtain
\[
 \nabla u_j(x)=-\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Omega\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^2}\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y
 -\int_\Omega\nabla_xH(x,y)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y.
\]
For fixed \(j\), \(\rho_j\) is bounded, the kernel \(|x-y|^{-1}\) is locally integrable in dimension two, and the regular term is uniformly bounded for
\(x\in\operatorname{supp} X\). Thus the double integrals below converge absolutely, and Fubini's theorem applies.
Interchanging \(x,y\) in the singular term gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\iint_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{X(x)\cdot(x-y)}{|x-y|^2}\rho_j(x)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y\\
 &\qquad=-\iint_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{X(y)\cdot(x-y)}{|x-y|^2}\rho_j(x)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y\\
 &\qquad=\frac12\iint_{\Omega\times\Omega} K_X(x,y)\rho_j(x)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The last equality is obtained by averaging the first two expressions. Therefore
    \begin{align}
    	\int_\Omega\rho_jX\cdot\nabla u_j
    	&=-\frac1{4\pi}\iint_{\Omega\times\Omega} K_X\rho_j(x)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y\\
    	&\qquad-\iint_{\Omega\times\Omega} X(x)\cdot\nabla_xH(x,y)\rho_j(x)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y.
    \end{align}
Comparing this with the integration-by-parts identity \eqref{eq:intpho_jXcdotnablau_j}, cancelling the minus signs, and dividing by \(M_j^2\) proves \eqref{eq:stress}.

For a compactly supported Lipschitz vector field \(X\), extend it by zero and mollify to obtain \(X_\ell\). The identity \eqref{eq:stress} holds for \(X_\ell\). Their supports can be kept in a fixed compact subset of \(\Omega\), with \(X_\ell\to X\) uniformly, \(\operatorname{Lip} X_\ell\le\operatorname{Lip} X\), and derivatives converging almost everywhere. For \(x\ne y\), we have \(K_{X_\ell}(x,y)\to K_X(x,y)\) and \(|K_{X_\ell}|\le\operatorname{Lip} X\). Dominated convergence therefore extends \eqref{eq:stress} to Lipschitz vector fields.

label: prop:square
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an atom \(a\) of \(\nu\), and write \(p=\nu(\{a\})>0\), \(\tau=\Pi(\{a\})\).
Choose \(\chi\in C_c^\infty([0,\infty))\) equal to \(1\) on \([0,1]\) and to \(0\) on \([2,\infty)\), and set
\[
 X_\varepsilon(x)=(x-a)\chi(|x-a|/\varepsilon).
\]
For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), this vector field is compactly supported in \(\Omega\). Direct differentiation gives
\(\|X_\varepsilon\|_\infty\le C\varepsilon\) and \(\operatorname{Lip} X_\varepsilon\le C\), with \(C\) independent of \(\varepsilon\).
If \(x,y\in B_\varepsilon(a)\) and \(x\ne y\), then \(X_\varepsilon(x)-X_\varepsilon(y)=x-y\), so \(K_{X_\varepsilon}(x,y)=1\).

To estimate the singular term, take \(0<\eta<\varepsilon\) with \(\nu(\partial B_\eta(a))=\nu(\partial B_{2\varepsilon}(a))=0\). This excludes at most countably many radii. Write
\(I_{j,\varepsilon}=\iint_{\Omega\times\Omega} K_{X_\varepsilon}\,\mathrm d\nu_j\,\mathrm d\nu_j\).
On \(B_\eta(a)^2\), the kernel \(K_{X_{\varepsilon}}\) equals \(1\), and the integral is exactly \(\nu_j(B_\eta(a))^2\).
When at least one variable belongs to \(B_{2\varepsilon}(a)\setminus B_\eta(a)\),
the bounds \(|K_{X_\varepsilon}|\le C\) and \(\nu_j(\Omega)=1\) show that the absolute value of the contribution is at most
\(2C\nu_j(B_{2\varepsilon}(a)\setminus B_\eta(a))\).
If \(x\in B_\eta(a)\) and \(y\notin B_{2\varepsilon}(a)\), then
\[
 |K_{X_\varepsilon}(x,y)|
 =\left|\frac{(x-a)\cdot(x-y)}{|x-y|^2}\right|
 \le\frac{\eta}{2\varepsilon-\eta}.
\]
The same bound holds after interchanging the variables. When both variables lie outside \(B_{2\varepsilon}(a)\), the kernel vanishes. Thus
\[
 \left|I_{j,\varepsilon}-\nu_j(B_\eta(a))^2\right|
 \le2C\nu_j(B_{2\varepsilon}(a)\setminus B_\eta(a))
   +\frac{2\eta}{2\varepsilon-\eta}.
\]
Letting first \(j\to\infty\) and then \(\eta\downarrow0\), we obtain
\[
 \limsup_j|I_{j,\varepsilon}-p^2|
 \le2C\bigl(\nu(B_{2\varepsilon}(a))-p\bigr).
\]
Finally, let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) through admissible radii; the right-hand side tends to zero.

For the regular term in \eqref{eq:stress}, \eqref{eq:greenbounds} gives
\[
 |B_{X_\varepsilon}(\nu_j)|\le C\|X_\varepsilon\|_\infty\nu_j(\Omega)^2\le C\varepsilon.
\]
For fixed \(\varepsilon\), the function \(\operatorname{div} X_\varepsilon\) is continuous and compactly supported, so weak convergence of \(\Pi_j\) yields
\(\int\operatorname{div} X_\varepsilon\,\mathrm d\Pi_j\to\int\operatorname{div} X_\varepsilon\,\mathrm d\Pi\). Moreover,
\[
 \operatorname{div} X_\varepsilon(x)
 =2\chi(|x-a|/\varepsilon)+\frac{|x-a|}{\varepsilon}\chi'(|x-a|/\varepsilon),
\]
This expression is uniformly bounded in absolute value, equals \(2\) at \(a\), and eventually vanishes at each \(x\ne a\).
Dominated convergence therefore gives
\(\frac12\int\operatorname{div} X_\varepsilon\,\mathrm d\Pi\to\Pi(\{a\})=\tau\).
Substituting these limits into \eqref{eq:stress} yields \(p^2/(4\pi)=\tau\).
Applying this equality to every atom and using the atomic decomposition from Lemma~\ref{lem:pressureupper} proves \eqref{eq:square}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Pull the normalized measures back to \(\mathbb D\), writing \(\nu_j^\mathbb D=(\phi^{-1})_\#\nu_j\) and \(\Pi_j^\mathbb D=(\phi^{-1})_\#\Pi_j\). For example, \(\nu_j^\mathbb D(B)=\nu_j(\phi(B))\) for each Borel set \(B\subset\mathbb D\). Define \(\nu^\mathbb D,\Pi^\mathbb D\) similarly. Set \(q_{n,j}=\int_\mathbb D z^n\,\mathrm d\nu_j^\mathbb D\). We first estimate their uniform decay as \(n\) increases.

The map \(\phi\) is Lipschitz on the closed disk. For \(z\ne0\), comparison with the boundary point \(\phi(z/|z|)\) gives
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(\phi(z),\partial\Omega)\le C\lvert\phi(z)-\phi(z/\lvert z\rvert)\rvert\leq C(1-|z|).
\]
Hence Lemma~\ref{lem:strip} implies \(\nu_j^\mathbb D\{|z|>t\}\le C(1-t)\) for \(t\) close to \(1\).
For \(t\) bounded away from \(1\), the same estimate follows from unit total mass after enlarging the constant.
Since \(|z|^n=\int_0^1nt^{n-1}\mathbf 1_{\{|z|>t\}}\,\mathrm d t\), Tonelli's theorem gives
\[
 |q_{n,j}|\le\int_\mathbb D |z|^n\,\mathrm d\nu_j^\mathbb D
 =\int_0^1 nt^{n-1}\nu_j^\mathbb D\{|z|>t\}\,\mathrm d t
 \le\frac C{n+1}.
\]
Thus the tails of \(\sum_{n\ge1}|q_{n,j}|^2\) tend to zero uniformly in \(j\). For fixed \(n\), \(q_{n,j}\) converges as \(j\to\infty\). Dividing \eqref{eq:moment} by \(M_j^2\), using \eqref{eq:square}, and passing to the limit, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:momentlimit}
 1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\left|\int_\mathbb D z^n\,\mathrm d\nu^\mathbb D\right|^2
 =\sum_i g(\phi^{-1}(a_i))p_i^2
 \le G_*\max_i p_i.
\end{equation}
The equality, whose left-hand side is at least \(1\), first shows that the set of atoms is nonempty. Since \(\sum_i p_i\le1\), only finitely many masses exceed \((\sup_i p_i)/2\), so the maximum is attained. The final inequality uses \(\sum_i p_i^2\le(\max_i p_i)\sum_i p_i\) and gives the stated lower bound.

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Values below \(A\).}
Fix \(0<b<A\). Since \(\nu(\overline B_{2r}(a))\downarrow p\) and \(bp<4\pi\),
we can first choose \(r\) sufficiently small and then \(\bar p>\nu(\overline B_{2r}(a))\) such that \(b\bar p<4\pi\).
Choose \(\alpha\in(b\bar p,4\pi)\). Lemma~\ref{lem:jensen} gives
\[
 \nu_j(B_r(a)\cap\{s_j\le b\})+
 \Pi_j(B_r(a)\cap\{s_j\le b\})\le C_{r,b,\bar p,\alpha,\Omega}\theta_j\to0.
\]
For \(0<\varepsilon<A\), take \(b=A-\varepsilon\). The \(\nu_j\) measure of \(B_r(a)\cap\{s_j<A-\varepsilon\}\) then tends to zero in the stated order of limits.
If \(\varepsilon\ge A\), the set \(\{s_j<A-\varepsilon\}\) is empty because \(s_j>0\).

\emph{Values above \(A\).}
Fix \(\varepsilon>0\), set \(h=A+\varepsilon\), and take any \(0<b<A\). Write
\(t_{j,r}=\nu_j(B_r(a)\cap\{s_j>h\})\). By \eqref{eq:pressure-comparison}, \(\,\mathrm d\Pi_j/\,\mathrm d\nu_j\le1/b\) on \(\{b<s_j\le h\}\), whereas this ratio is at most \(1/h\) on \(\{s_j>h\}\).
Combining this with the estimate above on \(\{s_j\le b\}\), we obtain, for fixed sufficiently small \(r\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pi_j(B_r(a))
 &\le o_j(1)+\frac1b\nu_j(B_r(a)\cap\{b<s_j\le h\})+\frac{t_{j,r}}h\\
 &\le o_j(1)+\frac{\nu_j(B_r(a))}b
       -\left(\frac1b-\frac1h\right)t_{j,r}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient \(1/b-1/h\) is positive. Move the term containing \(t_{j,r}\) to the left and let first \(j\to\infty\),
then \(r\downarrow0\) through radii satisfying \(\nu(\partial B_r(a))=\Pi(\partial B_r(a))=0\). By \eqref{eq:square},
\(\Pi(\{a\})=p^2/(4\pi)=p/A\), so
\[
 \lim_{r\downarrow0}\limsup_jt_{j,r}
 \le\frac{p/b-p/A}{1/b-1/h}.
\]
Finally, let \(b\uparrow A\). The numerator tends to zero, whereas the denominator tends to \(1/A-1/h>0\); hence the right-hand side tends to zero.
Together with the estimate for \(\{s_j<A-\varepsilon\}\), this proves \eqref{eq:height}. As \(r\) decreases, the \(\nu_j\) measure of \(B_r(a)\cap\{|s_j-A|>\varepsilon\}\) is nonincreasing.
Consequently, the limit as \(r\downarrow0\) is zero without restricting the choice of radii.

\emph{Convergence in total variation.}
Set \(h_j=(1-e^{-u_j^2})/s_j\). By \eqref{eq:ratios},
\[
 \left\|\Pi_j-\frac1A\nu_j\right\|_{\operatorname{TV}(B_r(a))}
 =\int_{B_r(a)}|h_j-A^{-1}|\,\mathrm d\nu_j.
\]
Fix \(b\in(0,A)\), and choose \(0<\varepsilon<A-b\). On \(\{s_j\le b\}\), the integral is at most
\[
 \Pi_j(B_r(a)\cap\{s_j\le b\})
 +A^{-1}\nu_j(B_r(a)\cap\{s_j\le b\}),
\]
which tends to zero by the estimate above on \(\{s_j\le b\}\). On \(\{s_j>b\}\cap\{|s_j-A|>\varepsilon\}\),
we have \(|h_j-A^{-1}|\le b^{-1}+A^{-1}\). By \eqref{eq:height}, the \(\nu_j\) mass of this set in \(B_r(a)\) tends to zero as first \(j\to\infty\) and then \(r\downarrow0\); so does the corresponding integral.
On the remaining set \(\{|s_j-A|\le\varepsilon\}\), use \(u_j=s_j/M_j\) and \(M_j\to0\), which follows from \eqref{eq:massbounds}, to obtain
\[
 |h_j-A^{-1}|
 \le\left|\frac1{s_j}-\frac1A\right|+\frac{e^{-s_j^2/M_j^2}}{s_j}
 \le\frac{\varepsilon}{A(A-\varepsilon)}+\frac1b e^{-b^2/M_j^2}.
\]
Since \(\nu_j(\Omega)=1\), letting first \(j\to\infty\) and then \(r\downarrow0\) bounds the upper limit of the total variation by
\(\varepsilon/[A(A-\varepsilon)]\). Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves \eqref{eq:TVheight}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Extend \(f\) by zero outside \(\Omega\), fix \(y\in\Omega\), and write
\[
 r=\sqrt{\frac{m}{\pi D}},\qquad
 f_*(x)=D\mathbf 1_{B_r(y)}(x),\qquad
 k_y(x)=\log\frac{L_0}{|x-y|}.
\]
Both densities have total mass \(m\). On \(B_r(y)\), we have \(f-f_*\le0\) and
\(k_y-\log(L_0/r)\ge0\); outside the ball, the signs are reversed. Hence
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_{\mathbb R^2}k_y(f-f_*)\,\mathrm d x
 &=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(k_y-\log\frac{L_0}{r}\right)(f-f_*)\,\mathrm d x\le0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The equality uses \(\int(f-f_*)=0\). The logarithmic singularity is integrable for bounded densities, so these integrals are well defined.
By \eqref{eq:greenbounds}, the Green potential is bounded above by \((2\pi)^{-1}\int k_yf\),
which is no larger than the value for the {density} \(f_*\). Integration in polar coordinates gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \frac D{2\pi}\int_{B_r(0)}\log\frac{L_0}{|z|}\,\mathrm d z
 &=D\int_0^r t\log\frac{L_0}{t}\,\mathrm d t\\
 &=D\left(\frac{r^2}2\log\frac{L_0}{r}+\frac{r^2}4\right)\\
 &=\frac m{4\pi}\left[\log\frac{\pi L_0^2D}{m}+1\right].
 \end{aligned}
\]
Since \(m/D\le|\Omega|\), we may choose \(L_0\) large enough such that \(r<L_0\). Taking \(C_\Omega=\pi L_0^2\) proves \eqref{eq:densitypotential}.

label: prop:strict
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:massbounds}, \(b_j=M_j^2\log(1/\theta_j)\) is bounded and eventually nonnegative. From any subsequence, extract a further one such that \(b_j\to b\ge0\) and \(\nu_j,\Pi_j\) converge weakly to \(\nu,\Pi\), respectively. Proposition~\ref{prop:atom} gives an atom \(a\) of mass \(p>0\); set \(A=4\pi/p\).
Fix \(0<\varepsilon<A\), choose \(r\) sufficiently small with both \(\nu\) and \(\Pi\) vanishing on \(\partial B_r(a)\) and \(\partial B_{2r}(a)\), and define
\[
 \eta_j=\nu_j|_{B_r(a)\cap\{|s_j-A|\le\varepsilon\}},\qquad m_j=\eta_j(\Omega).
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:height}, \(\liminf_jm_j\ge p/2\) for sufficiently small \(r\). {Set \(F_j=\Omega\cap B_r(a)\cap\{|s_j-A|\le\varepsilon\}\). Using \(\rho_j=\theta_ju_je^{u_j^2}\) and \(u_j=s_j/M_j\), the density of the restricted measure is
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d\eta_j}{\,\mathrm d x}
 =\mathbf 1_{F_j}\frac{\rho_j}{M_j}
 =\mathbf 1_{F_j}\frac{\theta_js_j}{M_j^2}
  \exp\left(\frac{s_j^2}{M_j^2}\right).
\]
On \(F_j\), we have \(0<A-\varepsilon\le s_j\le A+\varepsilon\), while this density vanishes outside \(F_j\). Thus, almost everywhere in \(\Omega\),
\[
 0\le\frac{\,\mathrm d\eta_j}{\,\mathrm d x}\le D_j:=
 \frac{\theta_j(A+\varepsilon)}{M_j^2}
 \exp\left(\frac{(A+\varepsilon)^2}{M_j^2}\right).
\]}
Symmetry of the Green function and \(s_j=M_j^2G\nu_j\) give
\[
 (A-\varepsilon)m_j\le\int s_j\,\mathrm d\eta_j
 =M_j^2\int G\eta_j\,\mathrm d\nu_j.
\]
Split \(\int_\Omega G\eta_j\,\mathrm d\nu_j\) into the parts inside and outside \(B_{2r}(a)\). Inside the ball, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:densitypotential} to \(G\eta_j\). Outside, the distance to \(\operatorname{supp}\eta_j\) is at least \(r\), so \(G\eta_j\le C_rm_j\). Substitution into the preceding inequality and division by \(m_j>0\) yield
\begin{align*}
 A-\varepsilon\le\frac{\nu_j(B_{2r}(a))}{4\pi}
 \biggl[(A+\varepsilon)^2-b_j-2M_j^2\log M_j
 +M_j^2\log\frac{C_\Omega(A+\varepsilon)}{m_j}+M_j^2\biggr]+C_rM_j^2.
\end{align*}
For fixed \(r,\varepsilon\), we eventually have \(p/3\le m_j\le1\), while \(M_j\to0\) and \(M_j^2\log M_j\to0\). Using \(\nu(\partial B_{2r}(a))=0\) and letting \(j\to\infty\), we obtain
\[
 A-\varepsilon\le\frac{\nu(B_{2r}(a))}{4\pi}\bigl((A+\varepsilon)^2-b\bigr).
\]
Letting next \(r\downarrow0\) and then \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) gives
\[
 A\le\frac p{4\pi}(A^2-b)=A-\frac{pb}{4\pi},
\]
Thus \(b=0\). Every convergent subsequence has this limit, so the first assertion holds for the full sequence. 

\begin{revision}
Combining \(M_j\to0\) with \eqref{eq:logenergy}, we obtain, for all sufficiently large \(j\),
\[
 0\le M_j^2E_j
 \le C'_\Omega\bigl[M_j^2+M_j^2\log(1/\theta_j)\bigr]\to0.
\]
\end{revision}
 Finally, \(\|\nabla s_j\|_2^2=M_j^2E_j\), and Poincar\'e's inequality yields the stated strong convergence.

label: eq:inversion
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix \(z_*\in\mathbb R^2\), set \(m(r)=\mu(B_r(z_*))\), and define
\[
 X_r(z)=\frac{z-z_*}{\max\{r^2,|z-z_*|^2\}},
 \qquad k_r(z)=\frac1{\max\{r,|z-z_*|\}}.
\]
The map \(X_r\) is Lipschitz and, away from the circle of radius \(r\), its divergence is
\(2r^{-2}\mathbf 1_{B_r(z_*)}\). It satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inversion}
 |X_r(z)-X_r(y)|\le |z-y|k_r(z)k_r(y).
\end{equation}
Translate \(z_*\) to the origin. When both points lie inside the ball, \(X_r(z)=z/r^2\), so \eqref{eq:inversion} holds. When both lie outside, a direct calculation gives
\[
 \left|\frac{z}{|z|^2}-\frac{y}{|y|^2}\right|
 =\frac{|z-y|}{|z||y|},
\]
which is the equality case of \eqref{eq:inversion}. If one point is inside and the other outside, assume \(|z|\le r\le|y|\). Squaring and cancelling the {cross terms}, the square of the left-hand side minus the square of the right-hand side is
\((|z|^2-r^2)(r^{-4}-r^{-2}|y|^{-2})\le0\), proving the inequality.

Choose \(r\) with \(\mu(\partial B_r(z_*))=0\). Multiply \(X_r\) by a smooth cutoff equal to one on \(B_L(z_*)\) and supported in \(B_{2L}(z_*)\), and smooth it near the circle of radius \(r\). The divergences converge off that circle and are uniformly bounded for fixed \(r\), so their integrals {with respect to} \(\mu\) converge. The corresponding kernels \(K_X\) are uniformly bounded, and \(\mu\) has no atoms. These approximations extend \eqref{eq:planarstress} to the chosen vector field. We may then remove the cutoff: the divergence error is \(O(L^{-2})\), and the kernels remain uniformly bounded for fixed \(r\). By \eqref{eq:inversion},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:massode}
 \frac{m(r)}{Ar^2}\le\frac1{4\pi}F(r)^2,\qquad
 F(r)=\int_{\mathbb R^2} k_r\,\mathrm d\mu=\int_r^\infty\frac{m(t)}{t^2}\,\mathrm d t.
\end{equation}
where the expression for \(F\) follows by integrating the identity
\[
 \frac1{\max\{r,|z-z_*|\}}
 =\int_r^\infty\frac{\mathbf 1_{\{|z-z_*|<t\}}}{t^2}\,\mathrm d t.
\]
{with respect to} \(\mu\) and applying Tonelli's theorem. The function \(F\) is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\), with
\(F'(r)=-m(r)/r^2\) almost everywhere.
Set \(f(r)=rF(r)\) and \(C=A/(4\pi)\). Almost everywhere,
\[
 m(r)\le Cf(r)^2,\qquad rf'(r)=f(r)-m(r)\ge f(r)-Cf(r)^2.
\]
Since \(\mu\) has no atoms, \(f(r)\to0\). Indeed, splitting the defining integral over a ball of fixed small radius \(\delta\) and its complement gives
\(f(r)\le\mu(B_\delta(z_*))+r\mu(\mathbb R^2)/\delta\). Let first \(r\downarrow0\), then \(\delta\downarrow0\), and use \(\mu(\{z_*\})=0\).
Choose \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), and then \(r_0\) sufficiently small that \(Cf(r)\le\varepsilon\) for \(r\le r_0\). Since \(f(r)>0\), integrating \(f'/f\ge(1-\varepsilon)/r\) from \(r\) to \(r_0\) yields
\[
 f(r)\le f(r_0)(r/r_0)^{1-\varepsilon},\qquad m(r)\le C_1r^{2-2\varepsilon}.
\]

The constants can be chosen independently of the center. Indeed, a finite nonatomic measure satisfies
\(\sup_{z_*}\mu(\overline B_\delta(z_*))\to0\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\). Otherwise, there would be balls whose radii tend to zero but whose masses have a positive lower bound. Since \(\mu(\mathbb R^2\setminus B_R(0))\to0\) as \(R\to\infty\), their centers must remain bounded. A convergent subsequence of centers would then yield a point every neighborhood of which has the same positive mass lower bound. Shrinking the neighborhood would give an atom, a contradiction. Thus \(r_0\) can be chosen uniformly, and \(f(r_0)\le\mu(\mathbb R^2)\) is also uniform. Since \(2\varepsilon<1\), interchanging the order of the nonnegative integrals gives
\[
 \sup_{z_*}F_{z_*}(0)
 \le C_1\int_0^{r_0}t^{-2\varepsilon}\,\mathrm d t+\frac{\mu(\mathbb R^2)}{r_0}<\infty.
\]
Returning to \eqref{eq:massode}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ballarea}
 \mu(B_r(z_*))\le C_2r^2
 \quad\hbox{for every center and all sufficiently small radii}.
\end{equation}
The argument so far applies to radii with \(\mu(\partial B_r(z_*))=0\). Approximating any sufficiently small radius from below by such radii and using continuity from below removes this restriction. If \(E\) is a Lebesgue null set, then, for any \(\eta>0\), it has a covering by small balls
\(E\subset\bigcup_\ell B_{r_\ell}(z_\ell)\) with \(\sum_\ell r_\ell^2<\eta\). Hence
\[
 \mu(E)\le\sum_\ell\mu(B_{r_\ell}(z_\ell))
 \le C_2\sum_\ell r_\ell^2<C_2\eta.
\]
Letting \(\eta\downarrow0\) gives \(\mu\ll\,\mathrm d z\). Write \(\mu=f_0\,\mathrm d z\). By the Lebesgue differentiation theorem, for Lebesgue almost every \(z\),
\[
 f_0(z)=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{\mu(B_r(z))}{\pi r^2}\le\frac{C_2}{\pi}.
\]

To ensure convergence at infinity, define the logarithmic potential
\[
 W(z)=-\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^2}
 \log\frac{|z-y|}{1+|y|}\,\mathrm d\mu(y).
\]
This potential is well defined on compact sets: the local logarithmic singularity is integrable {when multiplied by} a bounded density, while at infinity the logarithm is \(O_K((1+|y|)^{-1})\) for \(z\) in a fixed compact set. Its gradient is locally bounded, since \(|z-y|^{-1}\) is locally integrable {when multiplied by} a bounded density and is bounded away from the singularity. In the sense of distributions, \(-\Delta W=f_0\). The singular kernel is now absolutely integrable. Split the numerator \(X(z)-X(y)\) of \(K_X\) in \eqref{eq:planarstress} into two terms, interchange \(z,y\) in the integral containing \(X(y)\), and substitute the integral formula for \(\nabla W\). This gives
\[
 -\int_{\mathbb R^2} f_0\operatorname{div} X\,\mathrm d z=2A\int_{\mathbb R^2} f_0\nabla W\cdot X\,\mathrm d z
 \qquad(X\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)).
\]

The left-hand side is the action of the distributional gradient \(\nabla f_0\) on \(X\), so
\(\nabla f_0=2Af_0\nabla W\). Since \(f_0\) is bounded and \(\nabla W\) is locally bounded,
we have \(f_0\in W^{1,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}\). The function \(W\) is also locally Lipschitz. The Sobolev product and chain rules therefore apply and give
\[
 \nabla(f_0e^{-2AW})
 =e^{-2AW}\nabla f_0-2Af_0e^{-2AW}\nabla W=0.
\]
A local Sobolev function with zero distributional gradient on the connected plane is constant. Thus \(f_0=C_0e^{2AW}\), and \(\mu\ne0\) implies \(C_0>0\).
Since \(-\Delta W=f_0\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}\), we have
\(W\in W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) for every finite \(q\). Taking \(q>2\) yields
\(W\in C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}\). Combining this with \(f_0=C_0e^{2AW}\) and iterating Schauder estimates,
we find that \(W,f_0\) are smooth. The function
\(V=AW+\tfrac12\log(AC_0)\) then satisfies
\[
 -\Delta V=Af_0=AC_0e^{2AW}=e^{2V},
 \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2V}=A\mu(\mathbb R^2)<\infty.
\]
Theorem~\ref{tool:chenli} gives
\[
 f_0=\frac1A e^{2V}
 =\frac4A\frac{\lambda^2}{(1+\lambda^2|z-z_0|^2)^2},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:classdensity}.

label: prop:profile
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(\widehat\nu_j(\mathbb R^2)=1\), there is a locally weakly convergent subsequence \(\widehat\nu_j\rightharpoonup\mu\). For every fixed \(T>0\), the ball \(b_j+r_jB_T\) eventually lies in \(B_{\delta_j}(a_0)\). The weak convergence inequality for open sets and \eqref{eq:diagonal} give \(\mu(B_T)\le p\). Letting \(T\to\infty\), we obtain \(\mu(\mathbb R^2)\le p\).
By \eqref{eq:halfnormalization} and the weak convergence inequality for closed sets,
\[
 \frac p2=\limsup_j\widehat\nu_j(\overline B_1)\le\mu(\overline B_1).
\]
For fixed \(z\in\mathbb R^2\) and \(0<t<1\), the center \(b_j+r_jz\) eventually belongs to \(\overline B_{\delta_j/2}(a_0)\). If \(\widehat\nu_j(B_t(z))>p/2\), then the original ball \(B_{tr_j}(b_j+r_jz)\) would be admissible with radius \(tr_j<r_j\), contradicting minimality of \(r_j\). Thus \(\widehat\nu_j(B_t(z))\le p/2\), and
\[
 \mu(B_t(z))\le\liminf_j\widehat\nu_j(B_t(z))\le p/2.
\]
Letting \(t\downarrow0\) shows that every atom of \(\mu\) has mass at most \(p/2\).

Fix \(X\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)\), and use
\(X_j(x)=r_jX((x-b_j)/r_j)\) in \eqref{eq:stress}. The singular kernel is invariant under this scaling, the regular term is \(O(r_j)\), and
\(\operatorname{div} X_j(x)=\operatorname{div} X((x-b_j)/r_j)\). By \eqref{eq:diagonal}, replacing \(\widehat\Pi_j\) by \(\widehat\nu_j/A\) introduces an error in the divergence integral of at most
\[
 \tfrac12\|\operatorname{div} X\|_\infty
 \left\|\Pi_j-\frac1A\nu_j\right\|_{\operatorname{TV}(B_{\delta_j}(a_0))}=o(1).
\]
Hence, for each fixed \(X\),
\[
 \frac1{4\pi}\iint_{\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2} K_X(z,y)\,\mathrm d\widehat\nu_j(z)\,\mathrm d\widehat\nu_j(y)
 =\frac1{2A}\int_{\mathbb R^2}\operatorname{div} X(z)\,\mathrm d\widehat\nu_j(z)+o(1).
\]
Here \(\widehat\nu_j\) is extended by zero outside the rescaled domain \(\widehat\Omega_j\).
If \(z\in\operatorname{supp} X\) and \(|y|\) is sufficiently large, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tailkernel}
 |K_X(z,y)|\le C_X/|y|.
\end{equation}
Thus the contribution from pairs with at least one variable outside \(B_L\) is at most \(C_X/L\), uniformly in \(j\).

If \(\mu(\{z_0\})=q>0\), take
\(X_\varepsilon(z)=(z-z_0)\chi(|z-z_0|/\varepsilon)\), with \(\chi\) as in Proposition~\ref{prop:square}.
Use the same estimates over the inner ball, annulus, and exterior as in that proposition, with \eqref{eq:tailkernel} controlling the contribution at infinity.
Letting successively \(j\to\infty\), the inner radius \(\eta\downarrow0\), and \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), we obtain
\[
 \frac{q^2}{4\pi}=\frac qA.
\]
This forces \(q=4\pi/A=p\), contrary to \(q\le p/2\). Hence \(\mu\) has no atoms.

It follows that
\[
 (\mu\otimes\mu)\{(z,y):z=y\}=\int\mu(\{z\})\,\mathrm d\mu(z)=0.
\]
First insert fixed smooth compactly supported cutoffs in both variables. Approximation by finite sums of products of continuous functions shows that \(\widehat\nu_j\otimes\widehat\nu_j\) converges locally weakly to \(\mu\otimes\mu\). Within the cutoff supports, apply {the Portmanteau theorem} to the closed set \(\{|z-y|\le\eta\}\). Taking first the upper limit as \(j\to\infty\) and then letting \(\eta\downarrow0\), its mass tends to zero because the diagonal has zero \(\mu\otimes\mu\) measure. Since \(K_X\) is bounded, the corresponding integral also tends to zero.
Away from the diagonal, the kernel is continuous, so we may pass to the limit in the truncated integral. Finally, \eqref{eq:tailkernel} allows the cutoff radius to tend to infinity, giving \eqref{eq:planarstress}.

Lemma~\ref{lem:weakclassify} gives the density of \(\mu\) as
\((p/\pi)\lambda^2(1+\lambda^2|z-z_0|^2)^{-2}\). In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:parentmass}
 \mu(\mathbb R^2)=p.
\end{equation}
Since \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous, every circle has zero \(\mu\) measure, and \eqref{eq:halfnormalization} gives \(\mu(B_1(0))=p/2\). We have already proved that \(\mu(B_t(z))\le p/2\) for every center \(z\) and \(0<t<1\). Letting \(t\uparrow1\) and using continuity from below gives \(\mu(B_1(z))\le p/2\).
{If \(z_0\ne0\), the sets \(B_1(z_0)\setminus B_1(0)\) and \(B_1(0)\setminus B_1(z_0)\) have equal positive area. The density is strictly larger than its value at distance one from \(z_0\) on the first set and strictly smaller on the second, up to their boundaries. Hence \(\mu(B_1(z_0))>\mu(B_1(0))=p/2\), contrary to the bound for unit balls. Thus \(z_0=0\).} Finally,
\(\mu(B_1)=p\lambda^2/(1+\lambda^2)=p/2\) implies \(\lambda=1\), proving \eqref{eq:profile}.

label: eq:Wpotential
title: Proof
body_md:
In rescaled coordinates, subtract the {mean on the unit circle} from the Green representation formula for \(w_j=u_j/M_j\). The circular mean identity for the logarithm gives, on each fixed ball \(B_T\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Wpotential}
 W_j(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}
 \log\frac{\max\{1,|y|\}}{|z-y|}\,\mathrm d\widehat\nu_j(y)+O_T(r_j).
\end{equation}
The error is uniform for \(z\in B_T\). Indeed, in the difference of the regular parts, both values of the first variable lie in a fixed compact subset of \(\Omega\) and are \(O_T(r_j)\) apart, while \(\nu_j\) has unit total mass. As \(|y|\to\infty\), the kernel above is \(O_T(|y|^{-1})\). Since \(\widehat\nu_j(\mathbb R^2)=1\), the part of the integral over \(|y|>L\) has absolute value at most \(C_T/L\), uniformly in \(j\).
For \(y\) in a bounded set and every finite \(q\), the kernel depends continuously on \(y\) as an element of \(L^q(B_T)\). To see this, truncate the logarithmic singularity on \(|z-y|<\eta\). The truncated kernel is uniformly continuous, and the \(L^q\) norm of the truncation error is bounded by a constant multiple of
\((\int_0^\eta |\log t|^qt\,\mathrm d t)^{1/q}\), independently of \(y\). Cover the bounded set of \(y\)-values by finitely many neighborhoods on each of which the \(L^q\) distance between kernels is less than a prescribed positive number, and choose a subordinate continuous partition of unity. Approximating by the kernels at the neighborhood centers gives a uniformly small \(L^q\) error. The integrals of the {functions in the partition of unity} converge by weak convergence of the measures. Thus the kernel integrals converge in \(L^q\). Finally, letting the outer cutoff radius tend to infinity gives \(W_j\to W\) in \(L^q(B_T)\), with \(W\) obtained by integrating the kernel in \eqref{eq:Wpotential} {with respect to} \(\mu\).
Since the density of \(\mu\) is radial, so is this integral. Its {mean on the unit circle} is zero,
as follows directly from the circular mean identity for the logarithmic kernel.
Writing \(W=W(R)\), we deduce from \(-\Delta W=\mu\) and \eqref{eq:profile} that
\[
 -2\pi R W'(R)=\mu(B_R)=\frac{pR^2}{1+R^2},
 \qquad W'(R)=-\frac2A\frac{R}{1+R^2}.
\]
Integration gives \(W(R)=C-A^{-1}\log(1+R^2)\). The condition \(W(1)=0\) then yields
\(C=A^{-1}\log2\), proving \eqref{eq:Wlimit}. Moreover,
the inequality \(|z-y|\le(1+T)\max\{1,|y|\}\) gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Wlower}
 W_j\ge-C_T\quad\hbox{on }B_T.
\end{equation}

Take a fixed ball of positive \(\mu\) measure. Its intersection with \(\{|s_j-A|>\varepsilon\}\) has \(\widehat\nu_j\) measure tending to zero, so, for all sufficiently large \(j\), the ball contains a point where \(s_j\le A+\varepsilon\). The identity \(s_j=A_j+M_j^2W_j\) and \eqref{eq:Wlower} give
\(0\le A_j\le A+\varepsilon+C_TM_j^2\). Thus \(A_j\) is bounded.

We first prove that, for every fixed \(\alpha>0\) and \(T>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:alllinear}
 \int_{B_T}e^{\alpha(W_j)_+}\,\mathrm d z\le C_{T,\alpha}.
\end{equation}
Choose \(m>0\) with \(\alpha m<4\pi\). Since \(\mu\) is nonatomic, \(B_T\) can be covered by finitely many small balls \(B_\eta(z_0)\) {such that the corresponding closed balls of twice the radius have} \(\mu\) mass strictly less than \(m\). By the Portmanteau theorem, the corresponding \(\widehat\nu_j\) masses are also less than \(m\) for sufficiently large \(j\). On \(B_\eta(z_0)\), \eqref{eq:Wpotential} gives
\[
 W_j(z)\le C+\frac1{2\pi}\int_{B_{2\eta}(z_0)}
 \log\frac{C}{|z-y|}\,\mathrm d\widehat\nu_j(y).
\]
{Applying Jensen's inequality to a probability measure constructed as in the local argument of} Lemma~\ref{lem:jensen}, we bound the exponential integral by
\[
 C|B_\eta|+\frac Cm\int_{B_{2\eta}(z_0)}
 \int_{B_\eta(z_0)}|z-y|^{-\alpha m/(2\pi)}\,\mathrm d z\,\mathrm d\widehat\nu_j(y).
\]
The inner integral is uniformly bounded because \(\alpha m/(2\pi)<2\). Summing over the finite cover proves \eqref{eq:alllinear}; replacing \(W_j\) by \((W_j)_+\) adds at most the area of the set.

Set \(\kappa_j=k_j(A_j+M_j^2)\). We first show that \(\kappa_j\) is bounded. Fix \(B_T\), choose \(C_T\) from \eqref{eq:Wlower}, and let \(L=2C_T+1\). For indices with \(A_j/M_j^2\le L\), we have \(c_j\le LM_j\), hence
\[
 \kappa_j=r_j^2\theta_j(A_j/M_j^2+1)e^{c_j^2}\le C.
\]
For the remaining indices, \(s_j\ge A_j/2\) throughout \(B_T\), and the exponent in \eqref{eq:fj} is bounded below by \(-2A_jC_T\). Since \(A_j+M_j^2\le C_LA_j\), we have \(f_j\ge c_T\kappa_j\) there. Integration over \(B_T\) gives \(c_T\kappa_j|B_T|\le\int_{B_T}f_j\le1\), proving boundedness of \(\kappa_j\).

Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). On \(\{s_j\le A+\varepsilon\}\), the density formula \eqref{eq:fj} gives, for all sufficiently large \(j\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:truncdensity}
 f_j\mathbf 1_{\{s_j\le A+\varepsilon\}}
 \le C\kappa_j(1+(W_j)_+)e^{(2A+3\varepsilon)(W_j)_+}.
\end{equation}
For \(W_j\ge0\), use \(s_j=A_j+M_j^2W_j\le(A_j+M_j^2)(1+W_j)\), \(A_j\le A+2\varepsilon\), and \(A_j+s_j\le2A+3\varepsilon\). For \(W_j<0\), use \(s_j\le A_j\) and the fact that the exponential factor is at most one. By \eqref{eq:alllinear}, the truncated densities are uniformly bounded in \(L^q_{\mathrm{loc}}\) for every finite \(q\).

Fix a ball with \(\mu(B_T)>0\). Proposition~\ref{prop:height} gives \(\widehat\nu_j(B_T\cap\{s_j>A+\varepsilon\})\to0\). Indeed, the ball corresponding to \(B_T\) in the original coordinates eventually lies in every fixed small ball about \(a_0\); let first \(j\to\infty\) and then the fixed radius tend to zero. For \(q>1\), let \(q'=q/(q-1)\) be the conjugate exponent. H\"older's inequality gives
\[
 \int_{B_T}|s_j-A_j|f_j\mathbf 1_{\{s_j\le A+\varepsilon\}}\,\mathrm d z
 \le M_j^2\|W_j\|_{L^{q'}(B_T)}
 \|f_j\mathbf 1_{\{s_j\le A+\varepsilon\}}\|_{L^q(B_T)}\to0.
\]
Set \(\mathcal E_j=B_T\cap\{s_j\le A+\varepsilon\}\). By Proposition~\ref{prop:height}, for every \(\eta>0\),
\[
 \int_{\mathcal E_j}|s_j-A|f_j
 \le\eta\widehat\nu_j(B_T)
 +(2A+\varepsilon)\widehat\nu_j(B_T\cap\{|s_j-A|>\eta\}).
\]
The right-hand side tends to zero as first \(j\to\infty\) and then \(\eta\downarrow0\). Combining this with the preceding H\"older estimate gives
\[
 |A_j-A|\int_{\mathcal E_j}f_j
 \le\int_{\mathcal E_j}|s_j-A_j|f_j
    +\int_{\mathcal E_j}|s_j-A|f_j\to0.
\]
Since \(\int_{\mathcal E_j}f_j\to\mu(B_T)>0\), we conclude that \(A_j\to A\).

Boundedness of \(\kappa_j\) and \(A_j\to A>0\) imply boundedness of \(k_j\). Moreover, \(\liminf_j k_j>0\). Otherwise, a subsequence would satisfy \(k_j\to0\), hence \(\kappa_j\to0\); by \eqref{eq:truncdensity} and \eqref{eq:alllinear}, the \(\widehat\nu_j\) measure of \(B_T\cap\{s_j\le A+\varepsilon\}\) would tend to zero, contradicting its positive limit.
Choose a subsequence with \(k_j\to k\in(0,\infty)\), and then a further one with \(W_j\to W\) almost everywhere on every compact set. Thus \(s_j=A_j+M_j^2W_j\to A\) almost everywhere. For fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), we have \(\mathbf 1_{\{s_j\le A+\varepsilon\}}\to1\) and \(f_j\mathbf 1_{\{s_j\le A+\varepsilon\}}\to kAe^{2AW}\). A uniform \(L^q\) bound for some \(q>1\) ensures uniform integrability, so Vitali's convergence theorem gives local \(L^1\) convergence of the truncated densities. Since \(\int_{B_T\cap\{s_j>A+\varepsilon\}}f_j\,\mathrm d z\to0\), the densities \(f_j\) themselves converge locally in \(L^1\). Comparing with the density of \(\mu\) and the formula for \(W\), we find \(k=A^{-2}\), proving \eqref{eq:strongsource}.

Finally, take logarithms in the definition of \(k_j\) and multiply by \(M_j^2\):
\[
 M_j^2\log k_j
 =-2M_j^2\log(1/r_j)-M_j^2\log(1/\theta_j)
 -2M_j^2\log M_j+A_j^2.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:strict} gives \(M_j^2\log(1/\theta_j)\to0\). Also, \(M_j^2\log k_j\to0\) and \(M_j^2\log M_j\to0\). Using \(A_j\to A\), we obtain \(M_j^2\log(1/r_j)\to A^2/2\), as asserted in \eqref{eq:scalematch}.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set \(\mu_j=(\theta_jB_j^2e^{B_j^2})^{-1/2}\) and \(d_j=\operatorname{dist}(y_j,\partial D_j)\).
Since \(\log\theta_j=o(B_j^2)\) and \(\log(1/R_j)=o(B_j^2)\),
\[
 \log\frac{R_j}{\mu_j}
 =\frac{B_j^2}2+\frac12\log\theta_j+\log B_j-\log(1/R_j)
 =\frac{B_j^2}2+o(B_j^2)\to\infty.
\]

After rescaling the disk by \(\mu_j\), the right-hand side of the equation for \(u_j/B_j\) satisfies
\[
 0\le\frac{\mu_j^2}{B_j}\rho_j
 =\frac1{B_j^2}\frac{u_j}{B_j}e^{u_j^2-B_j^2}\le B_j^{-2},
\]
because \(u_j\le B_j\) in \(D_j\).

We first prove that \(d_j/\mu_j\to\infty\). If this ratio were bounded along a subsequence, rescale \(u_j/B_j\) by \(\mu_j\) about the nearest boundary point to \(y_j\). The rescaled functions lie between zero and one, their boundary supremum is \(o(1)\), and the absolute value of the right-hand side is at most \(B_j^{-2}\). Subtract the harmonic extension of the boundary values. The resulting functions are bounded, vanish on the boundary, and have right-hand sides tending uniformly to zero. By the maximum principle, the subtracted harmonic functions have supremum \(o(1)\).
Since \(R_j/\mu_j\to\infty\), the rescaled boundaries converge locally smoothly to a line, so the constants in local boundary estimates can be chosen independently of \(j\). If the rescaled distance of the maximum point from the boundary tends to zero, these estimates force its value to tend to zero, contradicting the normalized maximum value one. If the distance tends to a finite positive number, a subsequence converges locally up to the boundary to a bounded harmonic function on a half-plane, with zero boundary values and value one at the limiting maximum point. Odd reflection across the boundary gives a bounded harmonic function on \(\mathbb R^2\). Liouville's theorem makes it constant, and the zero boundary values force it to vanish, again a contradiction. Hence \(d_j/\mu_j\to\infty\).

The functions
\(\eta_j(z)=B_j(u_j(y_j+\mu_jz)-B_j)\)
are now eventually defined on every fixed ball and satisfy
\(\eta_j\le0=\eta_j(0)\) and \(0\le-\Delta\eta_j\le1\).
The local \(W^{2,q}\) and Schauder estimates at the beginning of Section~\ref{sec:local} give a subsequence converging in \(C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2)\).
Positivity of the Green function at the interior point \(y_j\), together with
\(\log(1/\mu_j)/B_j^2\to1/2\), shows as in Lemma~\ref{lem:maxbubble} that the limit \(\eta\) satisfies \(\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\eta}\le4\pi\). Here \(y_j\) stays in a fixed compact subset of \(\Omega\), and \(u_j\le B_j\) in \(D_j\), so the rescaled factor \((u_j/B_j)e^{u_j^2-B_j^2}\) is at most one. Theorem~\ref{tool:chenli} therefore gives \(\eta_j\to U\) in \(C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

To estimate the distance to \(\partial D_j\), let \(h_j\) be the harmonic extension of \(u_j|_{\partial D_j}\) to \(D_j\). Subscripts indicate the domain: \(G_\Omega=G\), while \(G_{D_j}\), \(H_{D_j}\), and \(R_{D_j}\) are the Dirichlet Green function of \(D_j\), its regular part with the sign convention \eqref{eq:green}, and its diagonal value. Subtracting the two Green representation formulas gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:differencegreens}
 h_j(y_j)=\int_{D_j}(G_\Omega-G_{D_j})(y_j,z)\rho_j(z)\,\mathrm d z
 +\int_{\Omega\setminus D_j}G_\Omega(y_j,z)\rho_j(z)\,\mathrm d z.
\end{equation}
By domain monotonicity and positivity of the Green function, every term on the right is nonnegative. With convention \eqref{eq:green}, the Robin function of the disk is
\[
 R_{D_j}(y_j)=-\frac1{2\pi}\log\bigl(d_j(2-d_j/R_j)\bigr).
\]
The explicit disk Green function also gives, for fixed \(T\), on \(B_{T\mu_j}(y_j)\),
\[
 H_{D_j}(y_j,z)=R_{D_j}(y_j)+O(T\mu_j/d_j)
 =R_{D_j}(y_j)+o(1).
\]
Indeed, after translating to a disk of radius \(R_j\) centered at the origin, its regular part is
\(-\frac1{2\pi}\log(|R_j^2-(y_j-c_j^*)\overline{(z-c_j^*)}|/R_j)\); 
The difference between this expression and its value at \(z=y_j\) is \(O(|z-y_j|/d_j)\).
The regular part for the original domain is bounded. In \eqref{eq:differencegreens}, retain only the integral over \(B_{T\mu_j}(y_j)\), with \(T\) fixed. The integral of \(\rho_j\) over this ball is \((m_T+o(1))/B_j\), so
\[
 \log(1/d_j)\le C B_j h_j(y_j)+C
 \le C B_j\sup_{\partial D_j}u_j+C=o(B_j^2).
\]
The same conclusion holds if \(d_j\) has a positive lower bound. For every fixed \(0<\sigma<1/2\),
\[
 \frac{e^{-\sigma B_j^2}}{d_j}
 =\exp\{-\sigma B_j^2+o(B_j^2)\}\to0,
\]
and hence \(B_{\exp(-\sigma B_j^2)}(y_j)\subset D_j\). On these balls, \(u_j\le B_j\), and we have already shown that the functions \(\eta_j\) obtained by rescaling about \(y_j\) by \(\mu_j\) converge to \(U\).
Apply the estimates from the end of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:maxbubble}. In the Green representation formula, first retain the integral over \(B_{T\mu_j}(y_j)\), and then use \(G(y_j,z)\ge\sigma B_j^2/(2\pi)-C\) on \(B_{\exp(-\sigma B_j^2)}(y_j)\setminus B_{T\mu_j}(y_j)\). The remaining integral is nonnegative and may be discarded. Letting first \(j\to\infty\) and then \(T\to\infty\) gives
\[
 B_j\int_{B_{\exp(-\sigma B_j^2)}(y_j)}\rho_j\to4\pi,
 \qquad \int_{B_{\exp(-\sigma B_j^2)}(y_j)}u_j\rho_j\to4\pi.
\]
Taking \(\sigma=1/32\) verifies the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:budget}. Lemma~\ref{lem:matching} with \(\tau=1/4\) then gives \eqref{eq:lowdiskmatch}.

body_md:
\label{lem:diskheight}
Let \(r_j\le\ell_j\to0\), and set \(D_j=B_{\ell_j}(b_j)\). Suppose that there are fixed constants \(c_0,C_0>0\) such that
\[
 c_0\le M_j^2\log(1/\ell_j)\le C_0,
 \qquad \sup_{\partial D_j}u_j\le C_0/M_j,
\]
Then \(\sup_{D_j}u_j\le C/M_j\).

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose, to the contrary, that a subsequence satisfies \(M_jB_j\to\infty\), where \(B_j:=\max_{\overline D_j}u_j\). The maximum is attained at an interior point \(y_j\), and
\[
 \frac{\log(1/\ell_j)}{B_j^2}
 \le\frac{C_0}{(M_jB_j)^2}\to0,
 \qquad
 \frac{\log(1/\theta_j)}{B_j^2}
 =\frac{M_j^2\log(1/\theta_j)}{(M_jB_j)^2}\to0.
\]
The boundary values are \(o(B_j)\), and the disks eventually lie in a fixed compact subset of \(\Omega\). Lemma~\ref{lem:lowdisk} therefore applies.

Set \(h_j=e^{-B_j^2/4}\). {By \eqref{eq:scalematch},
\[
 M_j^2\log\frac{h_j}{r_j}
 =-\frac{(M_jB_j)^2}{4}+M_j^2\log\frac1{r_j}
 \longrightarrow-\infty,
\]
so \(h_j/r_j\to0\).} Local weak convergence to the nonatomic measure \(\mu\) implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:smallballuniform}
 \sup_{z\in K}\widehat\nu_j(B_{\eta_j}(z))\to0
 \quad\hbox{for compact }K\subset\mathbb R^2\hbox{ and }\eta_j\to0.
\end{equation}
{Indeed, if the supremum did not tend to zero, there would be \(c>0\) and centers \(z_j\in K\), converging along a subsequence to \(z\), such that \(\widehat\nu_j(B_{\eta_j}(z_j))\ge c\). For every fixed \(t>0\), these balls eventually lie in \(\overline B_t(z)\). Portmanteau's inequality gives
\[
 c\le\limsup_j\widehat\nu_j(\overline B_t(z))\le\mu(\overline B_t(z)).
\]
Letting \(t\downarrow0\) contradicts \(\mu(\{z\})=0\).}

Fix \(T\) with \(\mu(B_T)>3p/4\). The ball \(B_{h_j}(y_j)\) in the original coordinates corresponds to \(B_{h_j/r_j}((y_j-b_j)/r_j)\). If this ball intersects \(B_T\), its center eventually belongs to \(\overline B_{T+1}\), so \eqref{eq:smallballuniform} bounds the \(\widehat\nu_j\) mass of the intersection by \(o(1)\). Thus
\[
 \nu_j(B_{Tr_j}(b_j)\setminus B_{h_j}(y_j))\ge p/2
\]
for all sufficiently large \(j\). Since \(r_j\le\ell_j\) and \(y_j\in D_j\), every point of \(B_{Tr_j}(b_j)\setminus B_{h_j}(y_j)\) is at distance at most \((T+1)\ell_j\) from \(y_j\). Write \(I_{\mathrm{out},j}=\int_{\Omega\setminus B_{h_j}(y_j)}G(y_j,z)\rho_j(z)\,\mathrm d z\). Restricting the integral to this set gives
\[
 I_{\mathrm{out},j}\ge\frac{pM_j}{2}
 \left(\frac1{2\pi}\log\frac1{(T+1)\ell_j}-C\right)
 \ge\frac c{M_j}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:lowdiskmatch} and local boundedness of the Robin function,
\[
 \frac{cB_j}{M_j}\le B_jI_{\mathrm{out},j}
 \le C+\log(1/\theta_j).
\]
Multiplication by \(M_j^2\) contradicts \(M_jB_j\to\infty\) and \eqref{eq:strict}.

label: eq:circle-oscillation
title: Proof
body_md:
We first estimate the oscillation of \(u_j\) on circles. For \(B_{R_1}(b_j)\Subset\Omega\) and \(0<R_0<R_1\), integration in polar coordinates gives
\[
 \int_{R_0}^{R_1}\int_0^{2\pi}
 |\partial_tu_j(b_j+Re^{it})|^2\,\mathrm d t\,\frac{\,\mathrm d R}{R}\le E_j.
\]
Hence there exists \(R\in[R_0,R_1]\) for which Cauchy--Schwarz on the circle yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:circle-oscillation}
 \mathop{\rm osc}_{\partial B_R(b_j)}u_j
 \le\sqrt{2\pi}\left(\int_0^{2\pi}|\partial_tu_j(b_j+Re^{it})|^2\,\mathrm d t\right)^{1/2}
 \le\left(\frac{2\pi E_j}{\log(R_1/R_0)}\right)^{1/2}.
\end{equation}

Fix \(T>0\), choose \(2+T<R_0<R_1\), and apply this estimate to the original radii in \([r_jR_0,r_jR_1]\). Since \(M_j^2E_j\to0\), we can select \(t_j\in[R_0,R_1]\) such that the oscillation on \(\partial B_{r_jt_j}(b_j)\) is \(o(M_j^{-1})\).
On the other hand, taking the circular mean in \eqref{eq:Wpotential} gives
\[
 \frac1{2\pi R}\int_{|z|=R}W_j\,\mathrm d\sigma
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int
 \log\frac{\max\{1,|y|\}}{\max\{R,|y|\}}\,\mathrm d\widehat\nu_j(y)+O_{R_1}(r_j).
\]
The absolute value of the logarithm is at most \(|\log R|\), so the mean of \(u_j\) on the selected circle is \(c_j+O(M_j)\). Set \(D_j=B_{r_jt_j}(b_j)\). Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:circlelow}
 \sup_{\partial D_j}u_j\le\frac{A+o(1)}{M_j}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:scalematch}, \(M_j^2\log(1/(r_jt_j))\to A^2/2\). Lemma~\ref{lem:diskheight} therefore gives a uniform upper bound for \(s_j\) on \(B_T\).

Return to \eqref{eq:fj}. On a fixed slightly larger compact set, we have \(s_j\le C\), \(A_j\le C\), \(k_j\le C\), and \(W_j\ge-C\), hence
\[
 f_j\le C e^{C(W_j)_+}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:alllinear}, the functions \(f_j\) are uniformly bounded in \(L^q_{\mathrm{loc}}\) for every finite \(q\). Interior \(W^{2,q}\) estimates for \(-\Delta W_j=f_j\), together with the \(L^q\) bounds for \(W_j\), yield local \(C^{1,\alpha}\) bounds when \(q>2\). The right-hand side of \eqref{eq:fj} then has uniform \(C^{0,\alpha}\) bounds on smaller compact sets, and Schauder estimates give \(C^2\) compactness. The known \(L^q\) convergence identifies every subsequential limit with \(W\); hence \(W_j\to W\) locally in \(C^2\).

The limit \(W\) has a unique strict maximum at the origin. Maximize \(W_j\) on a fixed small closed ball about the origin. Uniform convergence ensures that each such maximum point \(z_j\) is eventually interior and that \(z_j\to0\). Set \(x_j=b_j+r_jz_j\) and \(\beta_j=u_j(x_j)\). Then \(x_j\) is a local maximum point, and
\[
 M_j\beta_j=A_j+M_j^2W_j(z_j)\to A.
\]
Since \(M_j\to0\) and \(A>0\), we have \(\beta_j\to\infty\).

Furthermore,
\[
 r_j^2\theta_j\beta_j^2e^{\beta_j^2}
 =k_j(M_j\beta_j)^2 e^{\beta_j^2-c_j^2}
 \longrightarrow A^{-2}A^2 e^{2AW(0)}=4.
\]
Here \(\beta_j^2-c_j^2=(M_j\beta_j+A_j)W_j(z_j)\to2AW(0)\), and \(AW(0)=\log2\). Thus \(\mu_j/r_j\to1/2\), and
\[
 \beta_j\bigl(u_j(x_j+\mu_jz)-\beta_j\bigr)
 =(M_j\beta_j)\bigl(W_j(z_j+(\mu_j/r_j)z)-W_j(z_j)\bigr)\to U(z)
\]
in \(C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}\). For each fixed \(T>0\), changing variables on the original ball \(B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)\) gives \(\beta_j\int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}\rho_j\to\int_{B_T}e^{2U}\). Dividing by \(M_j\beta_j\to A\) and then letting \(T\to\infty\) proves the last assertion of \eqref{eq:scaleconstants}.
