title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:scalematch}, \(r_j/{\varrho_j}\to0\). Applying \eqref{eq:circle-oscillation} to radii in \([4{\varrho_j},8{\varrho_j}]\), we can choose \(\ell_j\in[4{\varrho_j},8{\varrho_j}]\) such that
\[
 \mathop{\rm osc}_{\partial B_{\ell_j}(b_j)}u_j
 \le\left(\frac{2\pi E_j}{\log2}\right)^{1/2}
 =o(M_j^{-1}),
\]
where the last equality follows from \(M_j^2E_j\to0\) in \eqref{eq:strict}.
To estimate the mean on this circle, set
\[
 \overline u_j(\ell_j)
 :=\frac1{2\pi\ell_j}\int_{\partial B_{\ell_j}(b_j)}u_j\,\mathrm d\sigma
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}u_j(b_j+\ell_je^{it})\,\mathrm d t.
\]
Choose a constant \(C\ge\max\{L_0,1\}\), depending only on \(\Omega\). The Green representation formula and Tonelli's theorem, applied to the nonnegative integrand \(G(b_j+\ell_je^{it},y)\rho_j(y)\), give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \overline u_j(\ell_j)
 &=\int_\Omega\left[\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
 G(b_j+\ell_je^{it},y)\,\mathrm d t\right]\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y\\
 &\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Omega\left[\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
 \log\frac{C}{|b_j+\ell_je^{it}-y|}\,\mathrm d t\right]\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y,
 \end{aligned}
\]
where we used \eqref{eq:greenbounds}. For each fixed \(y\), the circular mean identity for the logarithm yields
\[
 \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|b_j+\ell_je^{it}-y|\,\mathrm d t
 =\log\max\{\ell_j,|b_j-y|\}.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \overline u_j(\ell_j)
 &\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Omega
 \log\frac{C}{\max\{\ell_j,|b_j-y|\}}\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y\\
 &\le\frac{M_j}{2\pi}\log\frac{C}{\ell_j}
 \le\frac{M_j}{2\pi}\log\frac{C}{\varrho_j}\\
 &=\frac{\sigma}{2\pi M_j}+\frac{M_j\log C}{2\pi}
 =O_\sigma(M_j^{-1}).
 \end{aligned}
\]
 Combining this mean bound with the oscillation estimate gives
\[
 \sup_{\partial B_{\ell_j}(b_j)}u_j
 \le\overline u_j(\ell_j)+\mathop{\rm osc}_{\partial B_{\ell_j}(b_j)}u_j
 =O_\sigma(M_j^{-1}).
\]
Moreover, \(4\le\ell_j/\varrho_j\le8\), so
\[
 M_j^2\log\frac1{\ell_j}
 =\sigma-M_j^2\log\frac{\ell_j}{\varrho_j}\longrightarrow\sigma>0.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:diskheight} therefore gives \(\sup_{B_{4{\varrho_j}}(b_j)}u_j\le C_\sigma/M_j\).

Write \(m_T=\int_{B_T}e^{2U}\uparrow4\pi\). For fixed \(T\), the relations \(r_j/\varrho_j\to0\), \(|x_j-b_j|=o(r_j)\), and \(\mu_j/r_j\to1/2\) give
\(B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)\subset B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j)\) for all sufficiently large \(j\). The convergence after rescaling about \(x_j\) and \(M_j\beta_j\to A\) yield
\[
 \liminf_{j\to\infty}\nu_j(B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j))
 \ge\lim_{j\to\infty}\nu_j(B_{T\mu_j}(x_j))
 =\frac{m_T}{A}.
\]
Letting \(T\to\infty\) gives the lower bound \(4\pi/A=p\). Conversely, for every fixed sufficiently small \(t>0\) with \(\nu(\partial B_t(a_0))=0\), the ball \(B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j)\) eventually lies in \(B_t(a_0)\). Hence
\[
 \limsup_{j\to\infty}\nu_j(B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j))\le\nu(B_t(a_0)).
\]
Letting \(t\downarrow0\) proves \(\nu_j(B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j))\to p\).

Fix \(T>0\). The same rescaling gives
    \begin{align}\label{eq:m_T}
    	&\int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}u_j\rho_j\,\mathrm d x
    	=\int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}\theta_ju_j^2e^{u_j^2}\,\mathrm d x
    	\longrightarrow m_T,\\
    	&\nu_j(B_{T\mu_j}(x_j))
    	=\frac1{M_j}\int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}\rho_j\,\mathrm d x
    	\longrightarrow\frac{m_T}{A}.
    \end{align}
The pointwise bound established above gives
\[
 0\le s_j=M_ju_j\le C_\sigma
 \quad\hbox{on }B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j),
\]
Since \(u_j\rho_j\,\mathrm d x=s_j\,\mathrm d\nu_j\), we have
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:int_B_2rho_j-b_ju_jrho_j}
    	\int_{B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j)}u_j\rho_j\,\mathrm d x=\int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}u_j\rho_j\,\mathrm d x+\int_{B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j)\setminus B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}s_j\,\mathrm d\nu_j.
    \end{equation}
The remaining integral satisfies
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 0&\le\int_{B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j)\setminus B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}s_j\,\mathrm d\nu_j\\
 &\le C_\sigma\bigl[\nu_j(B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j))
 -\nu_j(B_{T\mu_j}(x_j))\bigr].
 \end{aligned}
\]
The mass convergence proved above and the {limit on the inner ball for fixed} \(T\) give
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:mass-converge-to-p-m_T/A}
    	\nu_j(B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j))-\nu_j(B_{T\mu_j}(x_j))
    	\longrightarrow p-\frac{m_T}{A}.
    \end{equation}
Combining \eqref{eq:m_T}, \eqref{eq:int_B_2rho_j-b_ju_jrho_j}, and \eqref{eq:mass-converge-to-p-m_T/A}, we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 m_T&\le\liminf_{j\to\infty}\int_{B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j)}u_j\rho_j\,\mathrm d x\\
 &\le\limsup_{j\to\infty}\int_{B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j)}u_j\rho_j\,\mathrm d x
 \le m_T+C_\sigma\left(p-\frac{m_T}{A}\right).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Finally, \(m_T\uparrow4\pi=Ap\), and \(C_\sigma\) does not depend on \(T\), so the error term \(C_\sigma(p-m_T/A)\) tends to zero as \(T\to\infty\). Letting \(T\to\infty\) in these bounds gives
\[
 \int_{B_{2\varrho_j}(b_j)}u_j\rho_j\,\mathrm d x\longrightarrow4\pi,
\]
which is the last limit in \eqref{eq:neighborhood}.

To verify the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:budget}, fix \(0<\sigma<A^2/64\). Since \(M_j\beta_j\to A\),
\[
 \frac{e^{-\beta_j^2/32}}{{\varrho_j}}
 =\exp\left\{-\frac{(M_j\beta_j)^2/32-\sigma}{M_j^2}\right\}\to0.
\]
Also, \(|x_j-b_j|=o(r_j)=o({\varrho_j})\), so \(B_{\exp(-\beta_j^2/32)}(x_j)\subset B_{2{\varrho_j}}(b_j)\) for all sufficiently large \(j\).
For fixed \(T\), we have \(T\mu_j/e^{-\beta_j^2/32}\to0\). Thus
\[
 \int_{B_{T\mu_j}(x_j)}u_j\rho_j
 \le\int_{B_{\exp(-\beta_j^2/32)}(x_j)}u_j\rho_j
 \le\int_{B_{2{\varrho_j}}(b_j)}u_j\rho_j.
\]
Letting first \(j\to\infty\) and then \(T\to\infty\), both bounds tend to \(4\pi\).
Moreover,
\[
 \frac{|\log\theta_j|}{\beta_j^2}
 =\frac{M_j^2\log(1/\theta_j)}{(M_j\beta_j)^2}\to0.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:representative}, the selected local maxima lie in a fixed compact subset of \(\Omega\), and the functions rescaled about them by \(\mu_j\) converge to \(U\). Together with the uniform bounds on the total mass and parameter, this verifies all hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:budget}.

body_md:
\label{prop:absorb}
For the local maximum points \(x_j\) selected in Proposition~\ref{prop:representative}, set
\[
 r_j^\circ=e^{-3\beta_j^2/16},\qquad
 I_{\mathrm{out},j}^\circ
 =\int_{\Omega\setminus B_{r_j^\circ}(x_j)}
 G(x_j,y)\rho_j(y)\,\mathrm d y.
\]
Then, for all sufficiently large \(j\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absorbconclusion}
 I_{\mathrm{out},j}^\circ\le C M_j,\qquad
 \theta_j\beta_j^2\ge c>0,\qquad
 M_j/\sqrt{\theta_j}\le C.
\end{equation}

title: Proof
body_md:
We suppress the subscript \(j\) when no confusion can arise and write
\[
 r=e^{-3\beta^2/16},\quad d=e^{-\beta^2/16},\quad
 Q=\int_{B_r(x_j)}\rho,\quad P_r=\int_{B_r(x_j)}P.
\]

\emph{The error estimate from the Pohozaev identity.}
For this calculation, translate \(x_j\) to the origin. The vector field
\[
 \mathcal T(x)=\frac{xP(x)}2+(x\cdot\nabla u)\nabla u-\frac x2|\nabla u|^2
\]
{satisfies \(\operatorname{div}\mathcal T=P\), as follows directly from \(-\Delta u=\rho\) and \(\nabla P=2\rho\nabla u\).}
On \(\partial B_r\),
\(\mathcal T\cdot n=\frac r2[P+(\partial_nu)^2-(\partial_\tau u)^2]\).
and therefore
\[
 P_r=\frac r2\int_{\partial B_r}
 [(\partial_nu)^2-(\partial_\tau u)^2+P]\,\mathrm d\sigma.
\]
Integrating the equation gives the mean normal derivative
\(\frac1{2\pi r}\int_{\partial B_r}\partial_nu\,\mathrm d\sigma=-Q/(2\pi r)\). Decompose the normal derivative into its circular mean and a mean-zero term to obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:defect}
 D:=P_r-\frac{Q^2}{4\pi}
 =\frac r2\int_{\partial B_r}
 \left[\left(\partial_nu+\frac Q{2\pi r}\right)^2
 -(\partial_\tau u)^2+P\right]\,\mathrm d\sigma.
\end{equation}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:neighborhood} and local comparison, the gradient of \(u-B_j\) is at most \(C/(\beta d)\) on \(B_d\). On each circle, the radial function \(B_j\) has constant normal derivative and zero tangential derivative.

Writing \(v=u-B_j\) and using the fact that the mean of \(\partial_nu\) on \(\partial B_r\) is \(-Q/(2\pi r)\), we have
\[
 \partial_nu+\frac{Q}{2\pi r}
 =\partial_nv-\frac1{2\pi r}\int_{\partial B_r}\partial_nv\,\mathrm d\sigma,
 \qquad \partial_\tau u=\partial_\tau v.
\]
Thus the difference between \(\partial_nu\) and its circular mean has absolute value at most \(2\|\nabla v\|_\infty\), while \(|\partial_\tau u|\) is at most
\(\|\nabla v\|_\infty\). Hence
\[
 \left|\partial_nu+\frac Q{2\pi r}\right|\le\frac{2C}{\beta d},
 \qquad |\partial_\tau u|\le\frac C{\beta d}.
\]
Comparison of the function values and \eqref{eq:meanexpansion} with \(\tau=3/16\) give \(u=(3/8+o(1))\beta\) uniformly on \(\partial B_r\). Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:defectbound}
 \frac{|D|}{r}\le\frac{Cr}{\beta^2d^2}
 +Cr\theta\exp\bigl(\max_{\partial B_r}u^2\bigr)
 =o(M^2).
\end{equation}
The first term is \(Ce^{-\beta^2/16}/\beta^2\). The exponent in the second is
\((-3/16+9/64+o(1))\beta^2=(-3/64+o(1))\beta^2\); 
and \(\theta\) is bounded. Both terms are \(o(\beta^{-2})\), while \(M\beta\to A>0\).
The choice \(3/16\in(2/16,1/4)\) ensures exponential decay of both error terms.

\emph{A test vector field from the gradient of a convex function.}
Fix \(\delta>0\) sufficiently small, and choose \(\chi\in C_c^\infty(B_{2\delta}(a_0))\) with \(0\le\chi\le1\) and \(\chi=1\) on \(B_\delta(a_0)\). Its support lies in \(\Omega\). For all sufficiently large \(j\), \(|x_j-a_0|<\delta/4\) and \(r<\delta/4\).
Set
\[
 Y(x)=\frac{x-x_j}{\max\{r,|x-x_j|\}},\qquad X=\chi Y.
\]
The vector field \(Y\) is the gradient of the convex function
\[
 \Phi_r(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 |x-x_j|^2/(2r),&|x-x_j|\le r,\\
 |x-x_j|-r/2,&|x-x_j|\ge r.
 \end{cases}
\]
so \(K_Y\ge0\). The identity
\[
 K_{\chi Y}(x,y)=\frac{\chi(x)+\chi(y)}2K_Y(x,y)
 +\frac{\chi(x)-\chi(y)}2
 \frac{(Y(x)+Y(y))\cdot(x-y)}{|x-y|^2}
\]
and \(|Y|\le1\) give \(K_X\ge-\operatorname{Lip}\chi\).
On \(B_r(x_j)^2\), the kernel equals \(1/r\).

For \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\), set
\[
 Q_\varepsilon=\int_{B_{\varepsilon r}(x_j)}\rho\,\mathrm d x,\qquad
 J=\int_{B_\delta(a_0)\setminus B_r(x_j)}
 \frac{\rho(y)}{|y-x_j|}\,\mathrm d y.
\]
Translate \(x_j\) to the origin and take \(|x|\le\varepsilon r\), \(t=|y|\ge r\). A direct calculation gives
\[
 (Y(x)-Y(y))\cdot(x-y)
 =|x|^2/r+t-x\cdot y(1/r+1/t)\ge t(1-2\varepsilon),
 \qquad |x-y|^2\le t^2(1+\varepsilon)^2.
\]
Thus \(K_Y(x,y)\ge(1-4\varepsilon)/t\).
Retain the pairs in \(B_r(x_j)\times B_r(x_j)\), together with the pairs between
\(B_{\varepsilon r}(x_j)\) and \(B_\delta(a_0)\setminus B_r(x_j)\) in both orders.
These three product regions are pairwise disjoint. Bounding the kernel on the remainder below by \(-\operatorname{Lip}\chi\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:interactionlower}
 \frac1{4\pi}\iint K_X\rho(x)\rho(y)\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y
 \ge\frac{Q^2}{4\pi r}+\frac{(1-4\varepsilon)Q_\varepsilon}{2\pi}J-C_\delta M^2.
\end{equation}

For each fixed \(j\), Lemma~\ref{lem:stress} applies to this compactly supported Lipschitz vector field. The regular Green term has absolute value at most \(C_\delta M^2\). Almost everywhere, the divergence satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{div} X=
 \begin{cases}
 2/r,&x\in B_r(x_j),\\
 |x-x_j|^{-1},&x\in B_\delta(a_0)\setminus B_r(x_j),
 \end{cases}
\]
and its absolute value is at most \(C_\delta\) on the cutoff annulus
\(B_{2\delta}(a_0)\setminus B_\delta(a_0)\).
By \eqref{eq:pressuretotal}, \(\int P=O(M^2)\). Thus, after multiplying \eqref{eq:stress} by \(M^2\), its right-hand side becomes
\[
 \frac{P_r}{r}
 +\frac12\int_{B_\delta(a_0)\setminus B_r(x_j)}
 \frac{P(y)}{|y-x_j|}\,\mathrm d y+O_\delta(M^2).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:interactionlower} and writing the difference of the two terms associated with \(B_r(x_j)\) as \(D/r\), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absorbmaster}
 \frac{(1-4\varepsilon)Q_\varepsilon}{2\pi}J
 \le\frac Dr+
 \frac12\int_{B_\delta(a_0)\setminus B_r(x_j)}
 \frac{P(y)}{|y-x_j|}\,\mathrm d y+C_\delta M^2.
\end{equation}
For fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), we have \(\varepsilon r/\mu_j\to\infty\). Convergence of the densities after rescaling by \(\mu_j\) gives
\(\liminf_j\beta_jQ_\varepsilon\ge4\pi\). Since \(Q_\varepsilon\le Q\) and \eqref{eq:flux} gives \(\beta_jQ\to4\pi\), the upper limit is at most \(4\pi\). Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qeps}
 \beta_jQ_\varepsilon\to4\pi.
\end{equation}

\emph{Splitting the weighted integral by function values.}
On \(\{u\ge\beta/3\}\), \eqref{eq:pressure-comparison} gives \(P\le3\rho/\beta\), so the contribution to the integral involving \(P\) in \eqref{eq:absorbmaster} is at most \(3J/(2\beta)\).

For the integral over \(\{u_j<\beta_j/3\}\), take
\[
 T=3A/8,\qquad q=5/2,\qquad q'=5/3.
\]
Since \(M_j\beta_j\to A\), the inequality \(u_j<\beta_j/3\) eventually implies \(s_j\le T\). Decrease the fixed \(\delta\) and choose
\(\nu(\overline B_{2\delta}(a_0))<\bar p<16p/15\). The identity \(Ap=4\pi\) then gives \(qT\bar p<4\pi\). Applying \eqref{eq:localjensen} and the truncation estimate \eqref{eq:lowheight-Lq}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lowLq}
 \left\|\mathbf 1_{\{u_j<\beta_j/3\}}\frac{P_j}{M_j^2}
 \right\|_{L^q(B_\delta(a_0))}\le C_\delta\theta_j.
\end{equation}
Since \(q'<2\) and \(|x_j-a_0|<\delta/4\),
\[
 \int_{B_\delta(a_0)}|y-x_j|^{-q'}\,\mathrm d y
 \le\frac{2\pi}{2-q'}(5\delta/4)^{2-q'}.
\]
H\"older's inequality therefore bounds the integral of \(P_j\), weighted by \(|y-x_j|^{-1}\), over \(\{u_j<\beta_j/3\}\) by \(C_\delta M_j^2\theta_j\).

Fix \(\varepsilon=1/100\). By \eqref{eq:Qeps}, the coefficient on the left of \eqref{eq:absorbmaster} is eventually at least \(9/(5\beta_j)\). The coefficient of \(J\) contributed by \(\{u_j\ge\beta_j/3\}\) is at most \(3/(2\beta_j)\). Moving that term to the left leaves a coefficient of at least \(3/(10\beta_j)\). Using \eqref{eq:defectbound} and boundedness of \(\theta_j\), we obtain
\[
 \frac3{10\beta_j}J
 \le |D|/r+C_\delta M_j^2+C_\delta M_j^2\theta_j
 \le C_\delta M_j^2.
\]
Thus \(J\le C_\delta\beta_jM_j^2\le C_\delta M_j\).

\emph{The outer integral and the parameter estimate.}
Outside \(B_\delta(a_0)\), the integration variable is at distance at least \(3\delta/4\) from \(x_j\), so this contribution to \(I_{\mathrm{out},j}^\circ\) is at most \(C_\delta M_j\). On \(B_\delta(a_0)\setminus B_r(x_j)\), the logarithmic upper bound for the Green function gives
\(G(x_j,y)\le C_\delta/|x_j-y|\), so the corresponding integral is at most \(C_\delta J\).
Hence \(I_{\mathrm{out},j}^\circ\le C_\delta M_j\). Take \(\tau=3/16\) in \eqref{eq:matching}. Since \(M_j\beta_j\to A\) and \(R(x_j)\) is bounded,
\[
 \log(\theta_j\beta_j^2/4)\ge-C,
\]
which proves \(\theta_j\beta_j^2\ge c>0\). Finally,
\[
 \frac{M_j^2}{\theta_j}
 =\frac{(M_j\beta_j)^2}{\theta_j\beta_j^2}\le C.
\]
This completes the proof.

body_md:
Suppose that the theorem fails, and choose positive solutions with \(E_j\ge j\). Lemma~\ref{lem:mass} and \eqref{eq:energyidentity} give \(M_j\le C_\Omega\) and \(\gamma_j\to\infty\). Proposition~\ref{prop:maxbound} yields \(\theta_j\to0\) and
\(\sqrt{\theta_j}\gamma_j\le C_\Omega\).

As in Section~\ref{sec:pressure}, pass to a subsequence along which \(\nu_j,\Pi_j\) both converge weakly. Proposition~\ref{prop:atom} shows that \(\nu\) has an atom of positive mass. Proposition~\ref{prop:representative} then provides local maximum points \(x_j\) associated with this atom. By Proposition~\ref{prop:absorb}, a further subsequence satisfies \(M_j/\sqrt{\theta_j}\le C\). Therefore
\[
 E_j\le\gamma_jM_j
 =(\sqrt{\theta_j}\gamma_j)(M_j/\sqrt{\theta_j})\le C.
\]
The constant may depend on the fixed atom and subsequence, but is independent of \(j\). This contradicts \(E_j\ge j\).

There is therefore a finite bound \(B_\Omega\), depending only on the fixed domain \(\Omega\), for which \eqref{eq:main} holds.
